articles.title: Iran Hits Back at Trump’s Threat of a ‘Crushing’ Economic ‘D-Day’ Campaign
articles.body:
Iranian officials have dismissed President Donald Trump’s threat to launch what he called the “most crushing economic operation”against Tehran, as the nearly six-month war enters a new phase of economic pressure and negotiations between the two countries remain stalled.
Trump announced the campaign late Wednesday, threatening consequences for countries that continue to provide Iran with access to global trade and financial networks.
“This will be economic warfare and isolation on an unprecedented scale,” he said. “Any country that allows its financial institutions, businesses, airports, or government entities to provide any type of lifeline to Iran will itself face tremendous economic consequences.”
Trump did not specify what specific measures would be imposed on countries that continue to do business with Iran. TIME has reached out to the White House for comment.
The President also called on U.S. allies to impose additional restrictions on Tehran in order to “cripple them and their ability to project terror worldwide.”
“This will be an economic D-Day, and we need all of our allies to stand with the United States of America to isolate, and defeat, the Iran threat,” he said.
D-Day commonly refers to June 6, 1944, Allied landings on the beaches of Normandy, France, which opened a major Western front against Nazi Germany.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Thursday the United States will impose "maximum economic pressure" on Iran.
"It is a one-two punch. We have the blockade (on Iran), and we are going to have the toughest sanctions in history," Bessent told CNBC. "It is going to work in Iran and we are going to collapse this regime."
How Iran responded
Iranian officials rejected Trump’s threats and instead pointed to the strains the conflict has placed on the U.S. economy.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi called the move a “diversion from America's own crisis: unprecedented debt & surging interest costs.”
“Doubling down on failed policies will only bring further defeat—and enmity of Iranians. U.S. economic terrorism threatens global economy and sovereignty worldwide,” he said Thursday morning.
The U.S. national public debt surpassed $40 trillion threshold this week.
Iran's deputy foreign minister Kazem Gharibabadi similarly took aim at Trump’s rhetoric, arguing that the President’s threats have become less relevant as the conflict, which began on Feb. 28, approaches its six-month mark.
“They claim Iran is on the brink of collapse and hanging by a thread, yet they beg all their allies to help them! The problem is the wrong calculations that, each time to cover them up, they’re forced to create a bigger failure for themselves,” he said Thursday on social media. “The military war didn’t yield results, so now they’ve named the next failure “economic war”.”
Trump has repeatedly used maximalist rhetoric during the war, previously warning that a “whole civilization would die” if Iran failed to meet a deadline for a deal in April and, more recently, weighing a "massive attack” against Tehran at the end of July.
Neither threat resulted in the action that Trump initially described.
The latest warning came a day after the United Arab Emirates (UAE), a major regional trading hub with Iran, announced that it would suspend trade with Iran following reported missile strikes.
Since the start of the war, the U.S. has imposed additional heavy economic sanctions on Iran as part of a “maximum pressure” campaign intended to restrict funding for Tehran’s military capabilities.
Some Iranian officials have responded by calling for the country to abandon its international nuclear commitments.
“The best response to Trump's escalation of the economic war is to withdraw from the NPT,” said Iranian member of parliament Ebrahim Rezaei.
The NPT, also known as the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, is an international agreement aimed at stopping the spread of nuclear weapons.
The Islamic Republic of Iran signed the treaty in 1968 and ratified it in 1970, committing as a non-nuclear-weapon state not to manufacture or acquire nuclear weapons.
Trump has repeatedly cited preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon as a justification for U.S. military action
“They have to get rid of it completely. They have to get rid of nuclear weapons. Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon,” Trump repeated Wednesday during the unveiling of the new White House helipad.
Where U.S.-Iran negotiations stand
Trump’s renewed economic threats come as negotiations between Washington and Tehran appear to have stalled amid disagreements over the Memorandum of Understanding (MOU), signed by both countries on June 17.
The document outlined commitments aimed at ensuring the full, toll-free reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, and established a 60-day cease-fire intended to allow technical talks to take place, including over Iran’s nuclear capabilities. Before the war, roughly a fifth of the world's global petroleum liquids consumptions passed through the waterway.
But Washington and Tehran have since offered differing interpretations of the agreement, and fighting resumed before the diplomatic process produced a broader settlement.
The dispute over the Strait has since reignited, with Iran releasing a list of six key demands that it says the U.S. must meet before the waterway can reopen.
Senior Iranian lawmaker Ebrahim Azizi on Thursday reiterated one of Iran’s demands to end America's “presence in the region immediately” and warned that “any further mistake or miscalculation will carry consequences far greater than before.”
Trump has dismissed the demands and instructed his representatives to seek compensation "for all of the people" that Iran has "killed and gravely wounded with their roadside bombs and many conflicts."
The 60-day threshold has now passed and there is little sign of a renewed cease-fire agreement.
“If Oman gets in the way, we’ll bomb the sh-t out of them,” Trump told Fox News reporter Trey Yingst on Monday.
China could present an even greater test of Trump’s economic strategy. The U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission stated that the country remains Iran’s largest trading partner and the primary buyer of Iranian oil.
When asked whether the sanctions would target China, Bessent responded: “Many conversations are best to have in private, and we are confident that everyone wants the Strait (of Hormuz) re-opened, and for energy prices to come back down,” adding “it would do them a big service to get with the program.”
Trump’s warning that countries doing business with Iran could face economic consequences raises questions about how the policy could affect Beijing as Chinese President Xi Jinping prepares to visit the U.S. next month.

articles.title: Trump’s threat to Oman signals more than the end of US diplomacy
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Trump’s threat to Oman signals more than the end of US diplomacy
Trump has threatened to “bomb the s**” out of Oman for the second time this year. A shocking repeat threat against a country that has served as a friend and mediator for the US for years.
What’s new about US power in the Middle East under Trump is not its destructive capacity, its blatant disregard for the lives of ordinary people, or its desire to keep oil and petrodollars flowing its way. No, all of this is simply how America operates. Trump is no aberration.
What is new is the absence of any diplomatic speak that paints over its violence and gags its belligerent confidence. Trump’s particularly fickle form of verbal vomit sees him adulate dictators in the same week he threatens his partners. The volatility of American discourse under his leadership compounds the anxiety and instability resulting from his behaviour.
Threats and more threats
Fox News reporter Trey Yingst said he had asked the president about parallel talks taking place between Iran and Oman about the control of the Strait of Hormuz, to which Trump replied: “If Oman gets in the way, we’ll bomb the s*** out of them.” In May, also speaking about opening the Strait, Trump made a similar threat: “Oman will behave like everybody else, or we’ll have to blow them up.”
The day after the latest threat, the White House shared Donald Trump’s Truth Social post on their official X account, with an image identifying the Strait of Hormuz as “New U.S. Territory,” echoing the president’s comment that “pretty soon I’ll be declaring the Hormuz Strait a territory of the United States.”
Encompassed within the identifying circle in the image of the Strait are not only Iranian territory but also Omani and Emirati territory. Crossing this key waterway requires ships to pass through the territorial waters of Iran and Oman, making Iran’s ability to close it and threaten international shipment a key thorn in the side of the president’s flesh.
Trump’s threats sound alarming in the world of diplomacy, even if no one expects him to actually bomb the Sultanate.
Why target a longstanding ally?
Today, Oman is appreciated as a country that has carefully cultivated its neutrality, allowing it to serve as a trusted mediator. It is credited with playing a key role behind the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), and Muscat has served as a vital backchannel between Washington and Tehran for years.
The Gulf country has also played an important role in the release of various American hostages in Iran and Yemen over the years.
This relationship emerges from a long history of friendship between the countries, with ties sitting among the longest of any Arab nation. These extend from the 1833 treaty of friendship and commerce between the two nations to the signing of the US-Oman Free Trade Agreement in 2006 (in effect since 2009) – one of the US’s only 20 bilateral FTAs worldwide.
This rich diplomatic history includes Oman being credited with dispatching the first Arab emissary to the United States in 1840 when Ahmad bin Na̔aman, special envoy of Sayyid Sa̔id bin Sultan (the Sultan of Oman and Zanzibar), visited New York. Not only this, but the first Arab head of state to make an official visit to Washington was Omani Sultan Sa̔id bin Taimur who met with US President Franklin Roosevelt in 1938.
Within this context, Trump’s threats to Oman appear puzzling. Both instances emerge as reactions to Oman’s role negotiating with Iran over access and navigation through the Strait. It’s not only Oman’s record of diplomacy and its proven status as a mediator with Iran, but also the geographic position that makes it both logical and necessary for the Gulf country to be involved.
Even more peculiarly, the June 17th 14-point Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding Between the United States of America and the Islamic Republic of Iran specified in point 5 that: “Iran will conduct dialogue with the Sultanate of Oman to define the future administration and maritime services in the Strait of Hormuz”. Observers had hoped the current dialogue would be a precursor to a renewal as the 60-day MOU was about to expire.
The agreement had already frayed by the beginning of July as Iran launched strikes on a number of ships and the US renewed its strikes on Iran for nearly two weeks. It was after this that Iran blatantly refused direct talks with the US, accusing it of first violating the terms of the MOU, and began talks with Oman.
Mediators Pakistan and Qatar were reportedly exchanging messages, but Iran has denied any negotiations. In the end, the deal expired.
Undermining peace
Oman’s independent policy toward Iran means it does not always align with US foreign policy, but this characteristic is what enables the country to facilitate dialogue and negotiations. Oman was in fact hosting nuclear talks between the US and Iran just before Trump and Netanyahu launched the war in February. Oman’s foreign minister Badr Al Busaidi tried to pre-empt this by publicly declaring that “a peace deal is within our reach” just the night before bombs started falling.
He later expressed his dismay that “active and serious negotiations [had] yet again been undermined,” referring to the launch of the 12-day war the previous year, which Israel started just two days before the sixth round of US-Iran nuclear talks were set to begin in Oman.
Trump is indeed upending the niceties of American diplomacy and rupturing long-standing relationships. He has recently given a cold shoulder to South Korea as he rekindles his love affair with Kim Jong-Un, has sided with Russia in UN resolutions on Ukraine, and has repeatedly made obnoxious, expansionist threats to make Canada the fifty-first state and seize control of Greenland. In that vein, Trump has already unilaterally renamed the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America and violated international law by abducting Venezuelan president Nicolas Maduro.
It’s muzzle off, open bullying.
No force of good
We might consider it a collapse of American diplomacy and its cover of democracy promotion around the world.
But let’s not kid ourselves. People who mourn the US’ role in the world are mourning an illusion. Authors have challenged this virtuous self-delusion for decades, trying to explain to Americans just why people hate America.
Indeed, the US in the Middle East was no force for good. Ask the Palestinians bearing the brunt of American support for Israel’s genocide in Gaza under Biden, Yemeni wedding attendees murdered by Obama’s drones, or the hundreds of thousands of children who died of starvation under Clinton-supported sanctions (infamously deemed “worth it” by then US ambassador to the UN, Madeleine Albright). The list can go on at length and extend well beyond the confines of the Middle East.
The US’ ongoing support for Israel’s genocide in Gaza and its war on Iran are only the latest episodes in what Marc Lynch has dubbed America’s “ruination of a region.”
Trump’s only stable regional pursuit may be expanding the number of Gulf signatories to the Abraham Accords, a desire that Kayhan Valadbaygi calls “low-cost US hegemony,” which positions Israel as its central military-security node.
The Accords are consistent with around four decades of USFP in the region, built on several goals. One includes fostering or forcing Middle East allies into relations with Israel – exemplified by the 1996 Qualifying Industrial Zones initiative, which gives goods produced in Jordan and Egypt duty-free access to US markets on the condition that they include Israeli inputs. The other goal is containing (previously Iraq and) Iran and its proxies. The war has exposed the failure of the latter.
Iran has not been contained, and this policy has had deleterious effects on people, communities, and regional security.
Oman’s foreign minister recently wrote that containment is a “myth” and “an error of nearly half a century” and has called for replacing containment with a new security logic to govern the region - one based on inclusion. This will require, in his assessment, “Gulf conversations for Gulf states” to reassess their ties with powerful allies like the US – “not to discard these…but perhaps to reset them” to match the realities revealed during the war. This avoidable war has forced an “essential” question for Oman and its GCC partners: which partnerships genuinely delivery security, and which "bring unwanted vulnerabilities.”
The unsettling difference in current US foreign policy is Trump’s unpredictability. Sandwiched between the US and Iran, Oman remains the only adult in the room – a stable mediator not retaliating in words but sufficiently confident to condemn poor behaviour and violations of international law.
Indeed, the region, middle powers worldwide, and the wider international community would benefit from considering Oman’s words. In fact, the region is overdue for a new security arrangement that takes into account the lives and aspirations of its people.
Crystal A. Ennis is a scholar of global political economy and international relations based at Leiden University, the Netherlands. She is author of Millennial Dreams in Oil Economies (Cambridge University Press, 2025).

articles.title: Gun stash in German forest believed to be linked to Russia, say reports
articles.body:
Germany is seeking to extradite a suspect from Romania over the discovery of an underground stash of weapons in a forest near Berlin that German media reports have linked to Russian intelligence.
Two weeks after German authorities found a drone carrying explosives at Leipzig airport, the interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, confirmed federal prosecutors had opened an investigation related to the secret cache of guns “on suspicion of preparing a serious act of violence that threatens national security”.
“This case demonstrates that we are operating under a high threat level,” he told reporters. As with the Leipzig incident, Dobrindt said he could not rule out the involvement of “foreign powers”.
Earlier, local media had reported that German authorities had unearthed two handguns and ammunition about a year ago in a wooded area outside the German capital after agents of the domestic intelligence service received a tip.
The find has been the focus of covert investigations by state security and counterespionage services on suspicion Russian intelligence was plotting assassinations on German soil, according to separate reports by Der Spiegel magazine and an investigative team led by Süddeutsche Zeitung.
Rather than removing the arms, German authorities left them on site after rendering them unusable in the hope they would lead to clues during a months-long electronic surveillance operation, Dobrindt said.
No one was observed trying to collect the weapons, leading investigators to believe the agent or agents had learned of the cache’s discovery and it was now “dead”.
Dobrindt described the suspect in Romania, whose nationality was not disclosed, as a “low-level agent” and noted several other such operatives had been detained so far this year.
Although the investigation into the Berlin stash has been long-running, the revelations apparently led Dobrindt to hastily call the news conference on Friday.
Sinan Selen, the head of the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution, Germany’s domestic intelligence agency, has warned for months of more aggressive tactics by Russian secret services, including plans for targeted attacks on German soil.
Moscow’s potential hit list is believed to include weapons contractor executives, opposition figures in exile and other prominent Ukraine supporters, according to the report by Süddeutsche and the public broadcasters NDR and WDR.
The federal prosecutor’s office and the Russian embassy declined to comment. A BfV spokesperson said: “As a matter of principle, we don’t comment on matters relating to any specific intelligence activities.”
Spiegel said German authorities were looking into possible links between the arms cache – a familiar Soviet tactic during the cold war – and a sabotage campaign against Ukrainian logistics routes blamed on Russia.
Last year Polish security officials arrested several people allegedly planning to mail parcels containing incendiary devices or detonators, some of them reportedly to have been posted from Romania.
Investigators believe the packages could have been remotely ignited or set off using timers during transit to do serious damage to vehicles, cargo planes or logistics centres and spread fear in the EU.
In 2024, a firebomb in a parcel posted via DHL exploded in a freight container on the tarmac at Leipzig airport. Only a delayed flight kept it from going off in the air.
Ukraine has been using the facility in Leipzig as an alternate location for the transport of military goods since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, according to official records.
This month the German newspaper Die Zeit reported that Russian secret services were plotting an attack against Stefan Thumann, the head of German drone manufacturer Donaustahl.
The report said German investigators were tipped off by a foreign intelligence service at the end of last year and arrested a Ukrainian man and a Romanian woman this spring.
Thumann is said to be under police protection. The case recalled reports in 2024 that US intelligence services had foiled a Russian plot to assassinate the chief executive of Germany’s leading arms manufacturer, in an apparent attempt to retaliate over the company’s role in providing armaments for Ukraine.
The plan to murder Armin Papperger, the chief executive of Rheinmetall, was reportedly one of several Russian government schemes to kill defence industry executives in several countries in Europe that have been supporting Ukraine’s war effort. The plot against Papperger was believed to be the most advanced.
Russia has repeatedly denied any involvement in sabotage, disruption or intimidation against EU member states.

articles.title: Inside The Domestic Radar Giving Ukraine Up to 250 Miles of Warning Against Russian Air Attacks
articles.body:
- Category

Inside The Domestic Radar Giving Ukraine Up to 250 Miles of Warning Against Russian Air Attacks
Ukraine’s domestically developed Pelikan radar can detect and track aerial threats at ranges of up to 400 kilometers, or roughly 250 miles, covering targets ranging from Shahed strike drones to cruise and ballistic missiles, according to an operator featured by Ukraine’s Air Command West on August 20.
Once a warning is received from a command post, the radar crew’s task is to detect the incoming target in its assigned sector as quickly as possible and relay the information across Ukraine’s air defense network.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The earlier a threat is detected, the more time Ukrainian air defense units and combat aircraft have to track and intercept it.
According to the operator, Pelikan is designed to work against significantly different types of targets, including relatively slow-moving Shahed drones, low-flying cruise missiles, and much faster ballistic threats.
“Pelikan is one of the most modern means of radar detection and surveillance. The radar operates at a range of 400 kilometers. Our main task is to detect an aerial target as quickly as possible: whether it is a Shahed, a cruise missile, or a ballistic missile. The earlier we detect it, the faster and more effectively our air defense and aviation can respond. Another equally important task is monitoring our aviation,” the radar operator said.
Beyond detecting incoming Russian weapons, the radar is also used to track Ukrainian military aircraft and help maintain a broader picture of activity in the airspace.
The 79K6 Pelikan was developed and produced by Ukraine’s Iskra Research and Production Complex, part of the country’s state defense industry.
Despite its long detection range, Pelikan is a mobile system. The radar weighs roughly 17 tons and can be deployed or packed up in as little as 30 minutes, allowing crews to relocate rather than operate permanently from a fixed position.
That mobility is particularly important in a battlefield environment where radar systems themselves can become high-value targets once their location is identified.
The arrival of the 79K6 in Ukrainian service back in 2016 also allowed S-300PT air defense units to operate more autonomously, giving them access to radar detection and tracking without relying entirely on other elements of the wider network.
Recently, Ukraine reportedly deployed the Swedish Saab 340 AEW&C, also known as the ASC 890, in operational conditions for the first time as it strengthens defenses against Russian missile and drone attacks.

articles.title: Press review: US tightens Iran pressure while Russia expands nuclear power projects abroad
articles.body:
MOSCOW, August 21. /TASS/. The United States is threatening broad sanctions against Iran; Donald Trump is pursuing renewed ties with Pyongyang as US-South Korea military drills are scaled back; and Moscow and New Delhi are developing alternative transport routes to accelerate bilateral trade. These stories topped Friday’s newspaper headlines across Russia.
Vedomosti: US seeks to tighten economic pressure on Iran with expanded secondary sanctions
US President Donald Trump has announced the launch of the "most crushing economic operation" against Iran. In a post on his Truth Social account, he threatened "massive economic consequences" for countries whose financial institutions, businesses, airports, or government agencies offer any assistance to Tehran. According to experts interviewed by Vedomosti, Washington has little scope for fundamentally new sanctions against Iran but could expand secondary sanctions against third-country entities and pressure Iran’s neighbors to restrict economic ties with Tehran.
Iran has been under sanctions imposed by the United States and its allies since 1979. Since the Middle East crisis began in late February, the United States has imposed a naval blockade of the Iranian coast and added 50 individuals, more than a dozen companies, and vessels that helped circumvent economic restrictions to its sanctions list.
It will be difficult for the United States to add anything new to the 26 executive orders issued by previous presidents, 10 acts of Congress, various targeted programs, and other sanctions measures against Iran adopted since 1979, BGP Litigation partner Sergey Glandin told the newspaper. "Everything that can be prohibited in transactions involving dollars, US persons, and Iranian persons has already been banned many times over," the lawyer said.
In theory, Glandin noted, Washington could try to block payments by a broader range of Chinese foreign trade entities on the grounds that they conduct transactions on behalf of or in the interests of parties linked to Iranian counterparties, thereby widening the criteria for becoming subject to secondary sanctions.
Amid US threats, the UAE government announced on August 19 that it was suspending all trade activity and financial transactions with the Islamic Republic. Turkey could potentially do the same, according to President of the Center for Middle Eastern Studies Murad Sadygzade.
However, there is potentially little the United States can do beyond expanding the number of secondary sanctions against individuals and entities in third countries that maintain contacts with Iran, Ivan Timofeev, Program Director at the Valdai Discussion Club, noted. "It is difficult to come up with anything qualitatively new," he said. According to Timofeev, Washington could try to force countries that share borders with Iran to close them through threats such as freezing Iraq’s oil export revenues held in US banks or imposing secondary sanctions. However, the United States currently lacks the technical capabilities to monitor land borders, Timofeev noted.
Kommersant: Trump renews outreach to North Korea with plans to meet Kim Jong Un
US President Donald Trump’s unexpected decision to reduce military exercises with South Korea in an effort to seek reconciliation with Pyongyang has been followed by another move. The White House chief has now said he will meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un this year. Kim Yo Jong, the North Korean leader’s sister, said she was unaware of any contacts between Kim and Trump on the matter but acknowledged that her brother retains "good memories and feelings" about the US president. Trump’s renewed outreach to North Korea could raise concerns among US allies about Washington’s reliability as a regional deterrent, Kommersant writes.
Trump mentioned a forthcoming meeting with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un on August 19, albeit somewhat in passing, while inspecting a new helipad at the White House and responding to a reporter’s question. The Wall Street Journal, however, reported with confidence that the White House chief is planning to meet with Kim during his trip to the Chinese city of Shenzhen for the APEC summit in November.
The president himself provided no details on the matter but again commented on the joint US-South Korean military exercises, which he had ordered curtailed less than 24 hours before they began on August 17.
A day earlier, Seoul announced that it was ending its annual Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises with the United States roughly a week ahead of schedule -- they had originally been due to conclude on August 27 -- "at the suggestion of the American side."
The South Korean leader has long sought to normalize relations with his northern neighbor, but to no avail: North Korea, which has formally enshrined in its constitution that the Republic of Korea is a "hostile state," has repeatedly rejected all of Seoul’s conciliatory gestures, Kommersant writes.
According to the newspaper, "Trump’s sudden focus on Kim and the scaling back of joint US-South Korean military exercises, of which Seoul was not even informed in advance, have clearly alarmed US allies across Asia." In the long term, experts warn, uncertainty about the United States as a deterrent to China and North Korea, which are expanding their nuclear capabilities, could push Japan and South Korea to develop nuclear arsenals of their own, the newspaper writes. Such discussions, although still occasional and largely conducted in private, are already taking place in both countries.
Izvestia: Russia expands nuclear power projects at home and abroad
Russia remains the only country in the world with expertise across the entire nuclear energy chain, Vladimir Putin emphasized at a meeting on August 20. Russia is also strengthening its presence on the global stage. Rosatom has already reached agreements to build 17 power units in six countries and is negotiating deals with another 15, potentially amounting to around 50 new agreements. The geographic scope of nuclear power units will also expand domestically, from the Urals to the Far East. Plans call for commissioning around 30 GW of new nuclear power capacity, including small nuclear power plants. Experts told Izvestia that Russia’s nuclear expansion depends on developing small modular plants and fourth-generation reactor technologies.
Russia continues to maintain its position as the undisputed global leader in the international nuclear power plant market. Rosatom’s export portfolio already includes 28 power units under construction in various parts of the world.
In addition, Rosatom is actively seeking to broaden its global presence. According to company CEO Alexey Likhachev, the state corporation has already signed agreements to build another 17 power units in six countries and is simultaneously negotiating with 15 countries, with expectations of reaching around 50 new package agreements.
Russia’s industry now faces an ambitious task: starting serial production of small nuclear power plants for both land-based and offshore deployment. This represents a serious technological challenge, as it requires research and development, the creation of new materials, and the introduction of innovations while ensuring strict nuclear safety, Deputy Chairman of the State Duma Committee on Industry and Trade Alexander Spiridonov told Izvestia.
Russia’s main technological advantage is its transition to fourth-generation nuclear power.
The transition to a two-component nuclear energy system is not simply about new reactors but about a fundamentally different raw-material framework, Nikita Illeritsky, Leading Research Fellow at the Institute of China and Contemporary Asia of the Russian Academy of Sciences and an energy expert, told Izvestia. According to him, conventional nuclear power plants use less than 1% of uranium, while the rest becomes waste. Fast-neutron reactors make it possible to reprocess spent fuel and reuse it in a closed cycle. As a result, what was previously considered waste becomes usable raw material. The main benefit is not an immediate reduction in the cost of a kilowatt-hour but strategic security: uranium utilization efficiency will increase by dozens of times, while the country’s accumulated reserves will be sufficient for centuries to come.
Izvestia: Russia, India develop new trade routes to strengthen economic ties
Moscow and New Delhi are exploring new ways to expand trade and economic cooperation. In particular, plans call for finally putting the Vladivostok-Chennai maritime corridor into operation. The two sides are discussing the development of capacity for handling energy resources and fertilizers, Russian Ambassador Denis Alipov told Izvestia. This would cut cargo delivery times from 40 to 24 days. However, launching the corridor could take up to 10 years, while its construction will require significant investment from both the government and the private sector.
"Moscow and New Delhi maintain regular contacts on establishing stable cargo flows along the Eastern Maritime Corridor (EMC). The agenda includes creating the necessary infrastructure and commercial capabilities, including the development of facilities in Vladivostok for handling oil, LNG, and fertilizers for shipment to India," Russian Ambassador to India Denis Alipov told Izvestia.
Anastasia Gavrilova, international relations specialist at the Higher School of Economics, noted that creating such an extensive network would require considerable investment from the government and major private businesses. However, projects of this kind are always geared toward the long term. A hub in Vladivostok would create an economic framework for cooperation between the two countries for decades to come, she added.
Russia has remained India’s largest oil supplier since 2022, surpassing Iraq, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE in terms of volumes, Izvestia writes. Under current conditions, the sudden disappearance of Russian crude oil would trigger a major shortage on the Indian market, according to Igor Yushkov, Leading Analyst at the National Energy Security Fund.
There are other options as well - the possibility of linking the route with the Trans-Arctic Transport Corridor is being discussed, which would link India’s eastern coast with Russia’s Northwest and Arctic zone.
"There are also favorable conditions for intensifying dialogue with New Delhi on India’s participation in the development of the Northern Sea Route," Alipov added.
The traditional route through the Suez Canal, the Bab el-Mandeb, the Strait of Hormuz, and European ports is currently vulnerable, logistically overloaded, and unsafe, Gavrilova noted. This is precisely why Russia and India are actively developing sovereign transportation arteries protected from external shocks.
Kommersant: Bitcoin rally may prove short-lived as investors await US policy signals
The sharp rise in bitcoin’s price on the evening of August 19 triggered record short-position closures, with total liquidations already surpassing $1.6 bln. The price increase is likely to be temporary, as investors await regulatory changes as well as a signal from the US Federal Reserve that it intends to cut its key interest rate, Kommersant writes. Institutional demand for bitcoin remains extremely low, as does activity among retail traders, amid its seasonal decline.
According to Coinmarket.cap, investments reached around $518 mln on August 19 alone, nearly 1.5 times the net inflow recorded for the entire month of July. Experts believe the reaction may have been driven by the outcome of US President Donald Trump’s meeting with representatives of the crypto industry, during which the White House chief reaffirmed his intention to push for passage of the Clarity Act in the US Congress - legislation designed to clarify cryptocurrency regulation among US agencies and make the industry more accessible to institutional investors.
The current increase in bitcoin’s price appears to be largely technical and is likely to prove temporary, as many investors are expected to move to lock in profits, market participants say. "The sharp closing of positions can temporarily push the price higher, but it does not indicate increased interest in the asset," Millpay Chief Operating Officer Igor Plotnikov said.
In the coming months, a key factor determining cryptocurrency prices will be the US Senate’s decision on the Clarity Act, which the current US president is actively backing, experts say.
"The bill is intended to create a clear regulatory framework for the US crypto market, but its passage has stalled in the Senate due to political disagreements, so if it is not adopted in September, pressure on bitcoin’s price will increase," Oleg Abelev, Head of the Analytical Department at Ricom-Trust Investment Company, told Kommersant. "Investors are counting on the bill’s passage because, without it, any current regulatory easing could easily be rolled back by a future White House administration," Dmitry Tsarkov noted.
Major investors are also waiting for "a clearer position from the Federal Reserve on cutting its key interest rate," Plotnikov noted.

articles.title: Israel confirms Apache squadron relocation to northern base
articles.body:
- Israel confirmed the permanent relocation of its 190th Apache squadron from Ramon to Ramat David airbase, one day after striking a Syrian air base linked to Turkish deployment plans.
- Israel said the August 18 strike on Abu al-Duhur was meant to prevent Turkish forces from establishing a presence near its border, a claim Syria and Turkey have disputed.
The Israeli Air Force has confirmed the permanent relocation of its 190th “Magic Touch” Squadron, an AH-64A Apache attack helicopter unit, from Ramon Airbase in the south to Ramat David Airbase in the north. A ceremony marking the squadron’s arrival was held at Ramat David, the military said in a statement posted to social media.
“The transfer of the squadron to Ramat David Airbase is intended to improve the availability of the combat helicopter fleet for defending the country’s borders by dispersing combat helicopter squadrons in the north and south,” the military said.
The confirmation lands one day after Israel struck the Abu al-Duhur air base in northwestern Syria’s Idlib province, hitting runways and storage facilities with eight airstrikes. Israel’s Prime Minister’s Office said the strike targeted preparations for a Turkish military deployment at the base, saying Syria was “on the verge of breaching” an agreed security status quo by allowing Turkish forces there. Turkey condemned the strike, and Syria’s foreign minister told Axios his government had no intention of hosting a permanent Turkish presence at the site.
The Abu al-Duhur strike marked Israel’s first attack on Syrian government assets since March, according to Al Jazeera, and has sharpened a standing rivalry between Israel and Turkey over influence in post-Assad Syria. Ankara has been training Syria’s army and helping rebuild state institutions since Bashar al-Assad’s fall in December 2024, according to i24NEWS. Israel’s concern centers less on Syria’s current military capacity and more on what a Turkish-backed Syrian military presence near its border could become, with radar, aircraft or air defense systems potentially restricting Israeli Air Force freedom of movement over Syrian airspace.
Ramat David sits roughly 20 kilometers (12 miles) southeast of Haifa, positioning squadrons based there for rapid response to threats from Lebanon, Syria and Iranian-linked proxies along the Golan Heights and Galilee. Before the 190th’s arrival, the base was primarily an F-16 hub, hosting three squadrons that have played a central role in Israeli air operations against Hezbollah in Lebanon and in Gaza, according to The War Zone.
For years, the Israeli Air Force kept both of its Apache squadrons, the 190th and the AH-64D-flying 113th “Hornet,” concentrated together at Ramon in the Negev desert. The new arrangement places a full Apache squadron permanently in the north for the first time in years.
The military’s public rationale for the relocation has centered on lessons drawn from the October 7, 2023, attack, when only four Apaches were on standby nationwide and Israel’s helicopter response depended on aircraft that happened to be forward-positioned at Ramat David that morning. During the war that followed, the 190th Squadron provided fire support to ground forces in Gaza and along the northern border, and took part in intercepting drones during confrontations with Iran, according to Ynet.
The squadron traces its history to 1980, when it was established at Palmachim Airbase flying MD 500 Defender helicopters, before moving to Ramat David and later Ramon as the Air Force restructured around the Apache in the 1990s. It has taken part in both Lebanon wars, the Second Intifada and multiple rounds of fighting in Gaza.

articles.title: SBU urges citizens to be particularly vigilant ahead of, on Independence Day
articles.body:
Under conditions of full-scale war, Russians may use mass events for Ukraine’s Independence Day to conduct shelling, provocations, terrorist attacks, sabotage, cyberattacks, and other crimes, the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) warns.
"The Security Service urges citizens to be vigilant and act responsibly regarding their own safety. On the eve of and during festive events, several basic rules should be observed: do not ignore air raid sirens and locate the nearest shelter in advance; do not approach suspicious objects and do not attempt to move or inspect them yourself; in case of detecting suspicious individuals, objects, or other signs of potential illegal activity, notify law enforcement," according to a statement on the SBU Telegram channel.
Citizens are also reminded not to publish photos or videos indicating locations of military personnel, critical infrastructure facilities, checkpoints, air defense assets, etc.; not to share information regarding the aftermath of strikes, air defense operations, or movements of Ukrainian troops; and not to fulfill requests from unknown individuals proposing doubtful tasks, including taking photos or videos of specific facilities, delivering packages, or leaving objects in designated places, even if they present themselves as law enforcement officers.
"Separately, the SBU draws citizens’ attention to attempts by Russian special services to recruit Ukrainians for preparing terrorist attacks and committing acts of sabotage. If unknown individuals offer money for arson, property damage, placing unknown objects, gathering information on military facilities, or other illegal actions, do not agree to such offers and immediately report them to the SSU," the Service emphasized.
In case of receiving information regarding preparations for sabotage, terrorist acts, recruitment, or other activities that may pose a threat to state security, citizens are asked to contact the SBU via the hotline at 1516, report via the "Burn the FSB Agent" chatbot, or email [email protected].

articles.title: German missile-carrier drone completes first flight
articles.body:
- POLARIS Spaceplanes flew its COBRA prototype for the first time, covering more than 20 km with a takeoff mass above 600 kg.
- COBRA is being developed with Diehl Defence under the AirLAS program to carry and launch IRIS-T air-to-air missiles from an unmanned aircraft.
POLARIS Spaceplanes has flown its COBRA prototype for the first time, covering more than 20 km in what the German company described as a smooth flight.
The German aerospace firm announced the milestone in a social media post, saying additional test flights are planned in the coming months and that video footage would follow in coming days. COBRA has a takeoff mass above 600 kg and is being developed jointly with Diehl Defence under the AirLAS program, an effort to build an unmanned aircraft capable of carrying and launching IRIS-T air-to-air missiles.
COBRA is intended primarily for air defense missions. Diehl Defence and POLARIS have described AirLAS as a way to fire IRIS-T missiles from an airborne platform rather than a fixed ground launcher, extending the missile’s reach and giving forces a mobile, forward-deployed option for engaging aircraft, drones, cruise missiles, or helicopters.
Diehl and POLARIS signed an exclusive cooperation agreement at the Paris Air Show in June 2025 to develop AirLAS. The two companies publicly unveiled a demonstrator called the Cobra 600 at the ILA Berlin air show in June 2026. That aircraft measured 6 meters long, used a delta-wing, flying-wing-style airframe with wingtip stabilizers, and was shown carrying a single IRIS-T missile on a top-mounted pylon. The version displayed at ILA Berlin was powered by two JetCat P1000-PRO micro turbojet engines, each producing just under 250 pounds of thrust, though the airframe includes intake ports for two additional engines.
The IRIS-T is a short-range, infrared-guided air-to-air missile built by Diehl Defence and used across multiple European and allied air forces. It weighs 87.4 kg (193 pounds), has a stated top speed of Mach 3, and a standard operational range of about 25 km (16 miles) when fired from an aircraft. Ground-launched versions of the missile family, IRIS-T SLS and IRIS-T SLM, have shorter reach, with ranges of roughly 12 km and 40 km respectively, according to figures the companies have cited.
By putting the missile on an unmanned aircraft, Diehl and POLARIS have said AirLAS is designed to move the launch point closer to a target before firing, rather than relying only on a missile’s own range from a stationary position. The companies have said the platform is designed to be recovered and reused after a mission, or expended as a one-way system depending on the requirement.
POLARIS Spaceplanes was founded to develop reusable hypersonic spaceplanes and describes COBRA as a scaled-down derivative of that spaceplane work adapted for defense applications. The company, based in Bremen, has separately worked on programs including the AURORA multipurpose spaceplane and received funding from Germany’s Federal Office of Bundeswehr Equipment, Information Technology and In-Service Support for in-flight refueling technology intended to extend range and payload capacity on its vehicles.
The AirLAS program has not been the subject of a confirmed procurement contract from the German military or any other government to date. Diehl Defence has said at least one unnamed country has expressed investment interest in the project, though no purchase agreement has been disclosed.

articles.title: Trump warns of ‘economic D-Day’ against Iran, but Tehran is well acquainted with sanctions
articles.body:
Trump warns of ‘economic D-Day’ against Iran, but Tehran is well acquainted with sanctions
NEW YORK (AP) — Nearing the six-month mark of the Iran war and facing diminishing stockpiles of key weapons, the Trump administration is touting a crushing financial campaign against Tehran, promising an “economic D-Day” against a country that has so far withstood nearly five decades of punishing American sanctions.
With sparse details, President Donald Trump announced this week that the U.S. would be imposing an “unprecedented” level of economic warfare and isolation on Iran, aiming to force its leadership to cave to demands to end its nuclear program and fully reopen the crucial Strait of Hormuz to oil and natural gas tankers.
It reflects the dire reality Trump faces with an increasingly unpopular war he can’t seem to end just months before pivotal midterm elections that will decide whether his Republican Party keeps control of Congress. Whether out of desperation or strategy, the president is refocusing America’s might on bringing Iran to its knees through an accelerated sanctions campaign against one of the most economically penalized countries in the world.
The immediate response from Iran hawks has been praise and a call for patience as it plays out, while other analysts warn that Trump is refusing to learn the lessons of his predecessors.
In an interview Thursday on CNBC, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent offered a small glimpse of what may be ahead, threatening secondary sanctions on nations and companies that conduct business with Iran.
He did not say exactly whom would be targeted as part of this next phase of the administration’s “ Operation Economic Fury, ” which earlier had focused on entities and individuals that buy oil from or bank with Iran. China and India, however, are major buyers of Iranian oil.
“If you insist on doing business with them, then the U.S. Treasury and U.S. government will put its full might and force against you,” Bessent said. “It’s time for our allies and the rest of the world to make a decision.”
Some experts see ‘uncharted waters’ that could force Iran’s hand
Despite decades of U.S. sanctions against Iran, the Trump administration is arguing that it’s only a matter of time and that striking the right economic target would get Tehran to its breaking point.
Richard Goldberg, who coordinated efforts to put diplomatic pressure on Iran in Trump’s first term, said the consequences of U.S. strikes on Iran’s nuclear sites last year, the war this year and the American naval blockade on Iranian ports have created the perfect storm for capitulation — one that didn’t previously exist.
“I think we’re watching a strategy, whether it takes a short time or a long time, that is very much about fundamentally changing the future of the world by seeing the end of this regime,” said Goldberg, who is now at the hawkish Washington think tank Foundation for Defense of Democracies.
“I caution everyone — including myself, who has worked on sanctions, who’s worked on financial warfare — to have the humility to admit that we are in uncharted waters,” he said.
He said the decision this week by the United Arab Emirates — once one of Tehran’s most important trading partners — to suspend trade with Iran over an alleged missile attack will only further isolate the government.
Beyond trade in domestically produced goods, the Emiratis had helped the country absorb some of the shocks caused by sanctions through its re-export hub.
Targeting allies and partners comes at a price
With nearly all of Iran’s energy, financial and transportation sectors already covered by U.S. sanctions, Trump’s aim appears to be to apply secondary sanctions on countries, including allies and partners, that have not cut all ties with Iran to starve the country of any remaining income it may still be receiving.
In many ways, it is a redux of Trump’s first-term “maximum pressure” campaign, which he has ramped up during his second term to include military action.
But as Trump and his allies discovered during his first administration, it can be difficult to enforce secondary sanctions without harming U.S. interests and provoking reciprocal measures. There were numerous instances of the administration granting sanctions waivers to countries, particularly those that rely on Iranian oil for their energy needs.
“Trump’s strategy now rests on targeting Tehran directly by impeding its touch points and access to the formal financial system and international economy,” said Behnam Ben Taleblu, senior director of FDD’s Iran program. “This will require making the Iran issue more important in U.S. bilateral relations with countries in Europe and Asia.”
Iran doesn’t see an ‘open door’ at the end of the sanctions campaign
Iranian officials and analysts have accused the Republican president of flip-flopping with his latest pivot to economic pressure against Iran. Trump has long derided past leaders who used sanctions to limit Iran’s ability to pay for its military and nuclear development.
In a post last week on X, Esmail Baghaei, spokesman for Iran’s Foreign Ministry, wrote that Washington’s pattern of retreating to sanctions when it doesn’t want to pursue diplomacy has proven to be futile.
“Iran has demonstrated over decades that it will not be strangled by these exhausted refrains,” he said. “The real risk is that American politicians, clinging to this bad habit, will instead strangle their own remaining chances of a less humiliating exit from a crisis of their own making.”
Ali Vaez, Iran director at the International Crisis Group, said the Trump administration’s decision to take its own “maximum pressure” policy to new heights with military action seems to ignore years of U.S. foreign policy lessons that show Iran does not respond well to pressure.
If anything, he says, the latest economic campaign has only “hardened Iran’s position.”
“I think (Trump’s) blind spot is the fact that the only thing that the Iranian regime views as more dangerous than suffering from U.S. sanctions is surrendering to U.S. terms,” Vaez said.
Plus, the past year of start-stop diplomacy has only worsened the already fragile dynamic between the longtime adversaries, Vaez says, adding that Iranian officials’ lack of trust in Trump and his mediators has created an untenable foundation.
“They believe that even if they capitulate to U.S. terms under economic duress, Trump would move the goalposts and ask for more,” he said. “And this is really the fundamental problem: Pressure without an open door is an exercise in futility.”
___
Associated Press writers Matthew Lee and Fatima Hussein in Washington contributed to this report.

articles.title: Ukraine Planned 1,000-Drone Swarm to Paralyze Moscow Airports
articles.body:
Ukraine drew up plans to unleash a swarm of up to 1,000 autonomous drones on Moscow’s airports in a bid to overwhelm Russian air defenses, cripple air travel and pressure the Kremlin back to negotiations.
The operation, codenamed “M&Ms,” was developed under former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov and envisioned sending hundreds of small, low-cost drones into Moscow in a single night, according to two sources familiar with the plan.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
According to The Atlantic report, the drones were designed to navigate and identify targets without human operators. Their onboard computers would contain detailed maps and images of designated targets, allowing the UAVs to compare live camera footage with data stored in their systems.
Once a target was identified, a drone would dive into it and detonate without requiring confirmation from an operator.
The goal: ground Moscow
The plan was designed to overwhelm Russian air defenses and disrupt Moscow’s four major airports – Domodedovo, Sheremetyevo, Vnukovo and Zhukovsky – potentially for an extended period.
Ukraine hoped prolonged disruption would force international carriers, including Turkish Airlines and Emirates, to reconsider flights to Moscow, cutting off a key link between Russia’s political elite and the outside world.
The operation was also intended to create pressure on Russian authorities and push President Vladimir Putin back toward negotiations to end Russia’s war against Ukraine.
Mariupol Volunteer Safe After Risking Everything to Save Son Allegedly Threatened by Russia’s FSB
The plan was reportedly presented to President Volodymyr Zelensky in early 2026. He raised concerns about the potential risks to civilian aircraft, passengers and airport workers but allowed preparations to continue, according to The Atlantic’s sources.
Organizers also proposed warning civilian airlines ahead of the operation so they could avoid Moscow’s airports and evacuate aircraft before the drone swarm arrived.
Project halted after Fedorov’s exit
Preparations were halted in July following Fedorov’s resignation as defense minister.
The sources said Fedorov had spent much of the year developing the project, assembling programmers to build the AI-based navigation system and securing funding from Ukraine’s European allies for autonomous drones.
The project could still be revived.
Zelensky’s office, however, denied the operation existed, calling the report “complete nonsense.”
The official said Ukraine has only one objective involving Russian airports: forcing Moscow to repeatedly impose its “carpet” emergency protocol, which restricts air traffic during security threats.
Ukraine does seek to shut Russian airports down for prolonged periods or even completely, the official said, but lacks long-range weapons precise and reliable enough to strike airports without posing excessive risks to civilians.
Russian airports have already faced repeated disruptions linked to Ukrainian attacks.
According to Russia’s Federal Air Transport Agency, restrictions were imposed 114 times between June 28 and July 28. Moscow’s four main airports accounted for at least 17 temporary shutdowns during that period.
Across Russia, more than 290 similar disruptions were recorded during the first quarter of 2026.

articles.title: Russian-Australian man charged over alleged operation to gather Ukrainian military secrets
articles.body:
Australian police have charged a 27-year-old Russian-Australian man with foreign interference after alleging he joined Ukraine's armed forces to obtain military information for Russian intelligence, the ABC reported.
Russia has repeatedly sought to obtain information about Ukraine's military through espionage and intelligence operations as it continues its full-scale invasion. The alleged operation also shows how Moscow can use individuals in third countries to gain access to Ukrainian military information and attempt to pass it to Russian intelligence.
The Australian Federal Police (AFP) arrested Vladimir Teslov on 20 August in Sumner, a suburb of Brisbane. He appeared in Brisbane Magistrates Court on 21 August, where his case was adjourned until 2 October, according to the ABC.
Alleged operation inside Ukraine
According to the AFP, Teslov traveled to Russia in October 2024 and underwent military-style training before returning to Australia in December.
Teslov allegedly maintained contact after his return with individuals he believed were connected to Russian intelligence services, the AFP said in a press release.
Police allege he traveled to Ukraine in May 2025 and joined the Ukrainian Armed Forces, where he gained access to information about Ukrainian military personnel, units, and locations.
The AFP alleges Teslov subsequently provided, or attempted to provide, information obtained in Ukraine to people he believed were acting on behalf of Russian intelligence.
The agency said he sought to collect and communicate information about Ukrainian military personnel, locations, and operations for the benefit of Russia.
AFP Commissioner Krissy Barrett said the alleged activity could have endangered Ukrainian troops.
“It is alleged that this conduct created a risk to the safety and security of Ukrainian military personnel,” Barrett said, according to ABC.
The allegations have not been tested in court.
Australia has been a major supporter of Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, providing about A$1.8 billion in military, economic, and humanitarian assistance.
“What happens in Ukraine matters in Indo-Pacific”: Australia pledged Ukraine another $70 million
Investigation into alleged Russian intelligence links
The AFP said its Counter Foreign Interference Task Force began Operation Woodcreeper in June 2026, following an extensive investigation by Australia's domestic intelligence agency, ASIO.
Australian authorities carried out searches at five properties in Queensland on 20 and 21 August, according to the AFP press release. Police seized electronic devices and other items relevant to the investigation, which will undergo forensic examination.
The AFP said further arrests are possible.
Barrett said there was no indication that Teslov posed a threat to Australia itself, although investigators allege parts of the activity took place both in Australia and overseas.
The foreign interference charge carries a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison.
The Russian Embassy in Canberra told ABC it learned of the case through media reports and had not received an official notification from Australian authorities or Teslov. It said it was using available channels to establish the circumstances of the case.
Russian espionage cases in Australia
Australian authorities have previously warned of Russian intelligence activity in the country.
ABC noted a separate case involving Russian-born Australian citizens Kira and Igor Korolev, who were arrested in 2024 and accused of attempting to gather and send sensitive information to Russia. Their charges were upgraded to conspiracy to commit espionage in June.
In 2022, Australian Security Intelligence Organisation (ASIO) Director-General Mike Burgess said the agency had disrupted a “hive of spies” from an unnamed country seeking to recruit Australians and obtain sensitive information. Multiple media reports later identified Russia as the country involved, although ASIO has not publicly confirmed this.
Last month, the Australian Signals Directorate and nearly two dozen international partner agencies warned that Russian-linked hackers were targeting Australian defense, communications, energy, and financial sectors.

articles.title: Iranian families struggle to afford the basics as US ratchets up economic warfare
articles.body:
Iranian families struggle to afford the basics as US ratchets up economic warfare
TEHRAN, Iran (AP) — Tehran’s grocery stores are well-stocked, but many families can barely afford the basics. Unemployment is soaring and those with jobs are working more hours for money worth half as much as a year ago, putting food, medicine and everything else — except for heavily subsidized gasoline — further out of reach.
“We have virtually given up on many things,” said Ahmad Karimi, 52, a taxi driver and father of two who has been working 15-hour days to make ends meet. “We’re cutting out fruit, we’re cutting out protein, we’ve given up leisure, we even work on weekends.”
Nearly six months into the war with the United States and Israel, the Iranian economy is taking a beating under the force of sanctions and a naval blockade that is making it extremely difficult for the country to export oil, its most valuable product.
Whether this intensifying economic pressure will translate anytime soon into military or political concessions from Iran remains to be seen — but some experts are skeptical. Since the war began, Iran has been attacking oil-rich neighbors and U.S. bases in the region, and disrupting shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, its biggest strategic advantage.
Iran is trying to use this retaliatory pressure — which is driving up energy prices globally — to bring the war to an end on the best terms possible. It is pressing for sanctions relief, and seeking enough control over the strait to demand payment from ships passing through to deliver energy and other goods.
The Trump administration — which is stuck fighting over a waterway in a war that was launched to curb Iran’s nuclear program — is now promising to deliver even tougher sanctions to try to squeeze the Islamic Republic into submission. But experts say U.S. President Donald Trump may be underestimating how long Iran can hold out.
Iran has been subject to Western sanctions for years and has become deft at partially circumventing them. It has expanded domestic production, used informal cross-border trade networks, bought restricted goods through third countries, and used a shadow fleet to transport its oil.
“Iran’s resistance capacity not only avoids collapse, it also prevents the economic pain from translating into the political pressure and changes that the U.S. expects,” said Hadi Kahalzadeh, an expert on Iran’s economy at Brandeis University.
Iran’s economic strains carry an ‘emotional toll’
Tehran’s sprawling Grand Bazaar is regularly packed with shoppers hoping to find more affordable staples than at the country’s grocery stores, where rice is 60% more expensive and beef is 150% more expensive than before the war.
A mother of two from northern Iran posted a photo on X this week after purchasing milk, eggs, toilet paper and a few other items, but no meat. She complained that it cost 89 million rials (about $65).
“Buying basic necessities has become our main priority, and our shopping basket has gotten smaller and more limited,” the 41-year-old told The Associated Press on condition of anonymity for fear of retribution.
“The emotional toll and the pressure we’re under are another story,” she said. “Every time we have to say no to our children, every time we have to go back and forth over a decision, whether it’s a class you’d love your children to take or something they really want you to buy for them, it’s genuinely exhausting.”
By the end of the year, inflation in Iran is expected to rise nearly 70%, according to the International Monetary Fund, and the country’s economy — devastated by a decade of sanctions before the war — is forecast to shrink by more than 5%.
While gasoline has remained cheap thanks to government subsidies, even that might not last forever as supplies get tighter. A presidential aide told Iranian state television last week that the country is now using more gasoline each day than it produces and may need to raise prices — something that in the past has led to widespread protests.
Iranians turn some anger toward countries behind sanctions
Iran’s theocratic leaders were already facing economic discontent before the U.S. and Israel started the war on Feb. 28. Protests had spread across the country at the beginning of the year before they were violently put down, with thousands killed and tens of thousands believed to have been arrested.
Many Iranians have now turned at least some of their economic frustrations toward the countries behind the sanctions and the attacks that have destroyed factories and critical infrastructure and killed scores of civilians, said Hassan Golmoradi, a Tehran-based economist.
“Despite the hardships and difficulties, they have shown considerable patience in putting up with the resulting economic pressures,” Golmoradi said.
Iran’s leaders have said it is a treasonous offense — punishable by death — to take part in anti-government protests.
“They do suffer, but they do not think that by joining violent protests they can achieve something for themselves and their families,” said Mohammad Farzanegan, a professor of Middle Eastern economics at the University of Marburg in Germany.
Trump is threatening tougher sanctions
On Wednesday, Trump vowed on social media to unleash against Iran the “most crushing economic operation ever taken against any country.” He also threatened secondary sanctions on nations and companies that continue to do business with Iran.
The United Arab Emirates, which for years had enabled Iran to circumvent sanctions and receive goods from other countries, announced this week it was suspending all trade with Tehran. Trump had called the leader of the UAE, Sheikh Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the day before the announcement.
With the economic struggles, the elected government of Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has said it favors a negotiated end to the war. “What concerns us is people’s livelihoods and their economic situation, and we are doing everything we can to deal with it,” he told reporters last week.
But the most powerful force in Iran remains the paramilitary Revolutionary Guard, which has only become stronger after withstanding U.S. and Israeli airstrikes that killed Iran’s top leaders during the war’s opening salvos. The Guard is pressing for greater concessions from the U.S., including Iranian control over the Strait of Hormuz and financial compensation for the war.
With negotiations to end the war stalled, Iran’s hard-liners believe their country can endure the conflict’s economic pressures longer than their adversaries.
Iran’s supreme leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, this month appointed a former Revolutionary Guard commander to head Iran’s powerful Supreme National Security Council, a sign that he favors the hard-line approach.
A taxi driver says something has to give
Official government statistics put Iran’s unemployment rate at 9.1%, though state-affiliated media outlets have said the real figure is most likely many times higher. A Labor Ministry official said last week that by late May, just three months into the war, more than 1 million jobs had been lost.
In a sign that Iran’s leaders are at least somewhat concerned about public opinion, the government has refrained from enforcing mandatory hijab regulations as harshly as it had been — a social freedom that has long been sought by many.
But these days many Iranians are focused on how their lifestyles are restricted economically.
Karimi, the taxi driver, said Iran’s leaders will need to do something soon to alleviate the financial pressures he and others are feeling.

articles.title: Ukraine planned 1,000 AI-guided drones a night to shut Moscow airports, Atlantic reports
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy allowed preparations for an AI-guided drone campaign against Moscow-area airports, The Atlantic reported on 20 August, citing two anonymous sources with direct knowledge of the proposal.
The reported plan sought to keep civilian flights grounded long enough to pressure Russia’s elite. Had it proceeded, it would have moved Ukraine toward large-scale autonomous strikes, raising questions under the laws of war about attacks without human confirmation. The Atlantic's disclosure follows months of reported Ukrainian attacks that repeatedly forced Moscow-area airport closures and sent increasingly large drone swarms toward the capital.
How the drone operation would have worked
Code-named M&Ms, the operation called for as many as 1,000 drones to fly toward Moscow-area airports each night and overwhelm Russian air defenses, one source said.
Onboard cameras would compare live views with preloaded maps and target images. They would also allow the drones to strike without pilot confirmation and to navigate without a remote-control link that is vulnerable to Russian electronic jamming, the sources said.
One source said prolonged airport closures were intended to pressure Kremlin-linked elites and push Vladimir Putin toward negotiations.
The plan was presented to Zelenskyy during the winter of 2025–26, The Atlantic reported. Preparations stopped after Zelenskyy dismissed Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, whom The Atlantic described as the operation’s mastermind, in July, both sources said. One source said another team could revive the project within about three months.
Both sources said Zelenskyy allowed preparations despite concerns that a drone could hit a civilian airliner. Planners proposed warning airlines, according to one source.
A Zelenskyy spokesperson declined to comment. Another unnamed presidential office official called the report “total nonsense,” saying Ukraine lacked long-range weapons reliable enough to strike the airports without posing undue risks to civilians.
Previous Ukrainian strikes on Moscow
The alleged M&Ms operation never launched, but other reported Ukrainian drone attacks repeatedly disrupted Moscow’s airports.
From 5 to 7 May 2026, restrictions imposed amid reported Ukrainian drone attacks delayed more than 450 flights at Moscow airports. Limits at Vnukovo remained in place for nearly 18 hours, EP reported, citing the independent Russian investigative outlet Agentstvo.
Earlier this week, Russian authorities claimed that 620 drones flew toward Moscow in one night, EP reported. The Atlantic placed Russia’s nationwide interception claim for that night at 791 drones. Ukraine’s military did not claim the attack.

articles.title: Chance of Iran war expansion dropped after Trump declared economic warfare, officials say

Security sources said on Friday that the chances of expanding the military confrontation with Iran in the near term have decreased, following a series of meetings and discussions with senior US officials.
According to the officials, US President Donald Trump’s decision to impose another harsh package of economic sanctions is intended to “buy time” until after the US midterm elections.
Accordingly, the IDF will increase its level of preparedness for the worst-case scenario of renewed strikes against Iran across all areas: intelligence, weapons procurement, interceptor production, target bank development, and Air Force readiness for both defensive and offensive operations.

Netanyahu responsible for final decision on Iran war

articles.title: British pilot teaching Americans to fly the F-35C
articles.body:
A Royal Navy officer has become the first British pilot to serve as an F-35C instructor and the first to be embedded within a United States Navy squadron flying the type, the Royal Navy has said.
Lieutenant Richard Woods, who grew up in Ashtead in Surrey, volunteered for a non-reciprocal exchange to Naval Air Station Lemoore in California, where he has been stationed since late 2023. At VFA-125 he instructs both ab initio US Navy and Marine Corps pilots and experienced aircrew training to become squadron instructors.
He said: “This level of joint training and integration between the F-35 partner nations at the tactical and operational level is essential. It’s needed to drive the ultimate objective of multi-national compatibility and integration in theatre.”
Britain operates the F-35B, the short take-off and vertical landing variant flown from the Queen Elizabeth-class carriers, rather than the C model. The Royal Navy has no carriers with catapults and arrestor wires, which makes the exchange one of the few routes by which a British pilot acquires conventional carrier expertise.
The C differs from the A and B principally in its much larger wing, which allows slower approach speeds for catapult launches and arrested landings and carries more fuel than either of its cousins. It also has a tail hook, strengthened landing gear and folding wings to fit the deck space available aboard an American carrier.
The route there
Lieutenant Woods completed officer training at Britannia Royal Naval College in 2014 and flew the Tucano on basic fast jet training with 72 Squadron at RAF Linton-on-Ouse before being selected for his first exchange, moving to Meridian in Mississippi in 2018.
Flying the T-45, he carrier qualified aboard USS Dwight D. Eisenhower and earned American gold wings, becoming what the US Navy calls a Tailhooker. Eighteen months later he moved to NAS Oceana in Virginia to convert onto the F/A-18 with VFA-106, the Rhino fleet replacement squadron, joining his front-line squadron VFA-211 on the F/A-18E in September 2020.
After working up with the squadron, including events at NAS Fallon under the eye of Topgun, he deployed aboard USS Harry S. Truman to the Mediterranean, a deployment that coincided with the Russian invasion of Ukraine. He was frequently entrusted with the ship’s defensive counter air alert lead, ready to launch and defend the carrier strike group at short notice, armed with AIM-120 and AIM-9X missiles and the Super Hornet’s 20mm cannon. He also flew enhanced air policing over Romania.
During the same deployment he flew dissimilar air combat training against RAF Typhoons operating from Cyprus, and spent several weeks with Spanish Typhoons on a detachment to Seville, instructing front-line Spanish pilots in one versus one and two versus one fighter manoeuvring. He said: “One of my most memorable exercises during deployment was leading a training sortie with Greek F-16s. We executed Defensive Counter Air from the USS Harry S. Truman, while Greek F-16s acted as the aggressors. All of it was to the incredible backdrop of the snow-covered mountain peaks of Crete.”
He finished his front-line tour with almost 300 carrier deck landings.
At Lemoore
Alongside instructing, Lieutenant Woods is assistant operations officer at VFA-125, responsible for planning and managing training across the squadron, liaising between its maintenance and training departments and managing its range space.
His advice to aspiring pilots was direct, he said: “Work hard and never give up. Stay focused working towards each objective along the way, but don’t lose sight of what you’re trying to achieve. It doesn’t happen overnight, but you’ll get there if you persevere.”
He said he hopes more Royal Navy pilots will follow, adding: “By training together, we ensure that we’re ready to stand together, if the time arises.”
Exchange postings of this kind have long underpinned British carrier aviation. When the Royal Navy retired the Harrier in 2010 and lost fixed-wing carrier flying altogether, a cadre of pilots was kept current by flying with the US Navy and Marine Corps, and that arrangement preserved the skills needed to regenerate the capability when the Queen Elizabeth class entered service.
