articles.title: Ukraine fields new jet-powered interceptor to counter Russian drones
articles.body:
- Ukraine's Defense Forces have fielded the Alexa Spatium, a jet-powered interceptor drone aimed at Russia's Geran-3, Geran-4, Geran-5, and Shahed-131 drones.
- The system joins a growing field of Ukrainian turbojet interceptors, including SkyFall's JetKiller and Firebolt Engineering's Griffen, developed to counter faster Russian drones.
Ukraine’s Defense Forces have added the Alexa Spatium, a jet-powered drone built to intercept small aerial, ground, and surface targets, to their arsenal, according to a Ukrainian defense outlet on Aug. 21.
The turbojet-powered aircraft was developed by Ukrainian engineers specifically to counter fast, low-flying threats in combat conditions. Its primary targets are Russia’s Shahed-type jet-powered Geran-3, Geran-4, and Geran-5 attack drones, along with the propeller-driven Shahed-131. The manufacturer says the system can also be used against reconnaissance drones, helicopters, and other individual targets, though it has not disclosed the name of the company that built it.
Alexa Spatium measures roughly 1.5 by 1.7 meters and launches from a mobile catapult within minutes of setup. The airframe is built from a lightweight composite material intended to allow sharp maneuvers without losing control. According to specifications the manufacturer says were confirmed during testing, the drone carries a turbojet engine, operates across low to medium altitudes, and can be flown either to preset coordinates or guided directly by an operator. It reportedly carries interchangeable warheads, listed as fragmentation-blast, shaped-charge, and thermobaric types, and uses television and infrared sensors to search for and track targets. The manufacturer says a drone that fails to complete its mission can return to its launch point for reuse.
The system enters service as Russia expands its use of jet-powered strike drones. Ukraine’s military intelligence agency HUR has said the Geran-3 uses a turbojet engine to reach speeds up to 370 km/h (230 mph), roughly double the speed of the propeller-driven Geran-2 that has formed the bulk of Russia’s long-range drone campaign since 2022. Ukrainian Commander-in-Chief Oleksandr Syrskyi said in June that Russia plans to raise the share of jet-powered drones in its strikes to 50 percent.
Ukraine has fielded a growing number of jet-powered interceptors this year to counter that shift. SkyFall has introduced the P1-SUN “JetKiller,” rated at roughly 370 km/h with a claimed 15-minute endurance. Firebolt Engineering’s Griffen interceptor, which the company says flies faster than 350 km/h at altitudes above 7,500 meters (24,600 feet), was credited by the Armed Forces of Ukraine with the country’s first confirmed jet-on-jet drone interception in early July. Former Deputy Prime Minister Mykhailo Fedorov said in mid-August that a separate Ukrainian manufacturer was running combat trials on an interceptor capable of exceeding 600 km/h (375 mph), though he did not name the system at the time.
Most of Ukraine’s earlier interceptor drones, including the widely used Sting, relied on propeller propulsion and cost as little as $2,500 per unit, according to figures previously reported by manufacturers. Those systems have downed the majority of slower Shahed and Geran-2 drones over the course of the war but have struggled against faster jet-powered variants, prompting the shift toward turbojet designs across multiple Ukrainian manufacturers.
The manufacturer describes Alexa Spatium’s mobility as a design priority, saying the full launch complex fits in a pickup truck and requires minimal position preparation. It also says the system uses a modular construction and automated launch sequencing, with preparation and firing handled remotely.

articles.title: Italy’s largest arms maker had no plans for a Ukraine factory—a year later, it has a Kyiv subsidiary
articles.body:
Italian defense giant Leonardo has quietly registered a research subsidiary in Kyiv, planting a direct corporate flag in Ukraine's wartime defense ecosystem, Euractiv reported. The move reverses the company's previous public stance against opening operations in Ukraine.
European defense firms are quickly embedding inside Ukraine's defense industry, as Ukraine's wartime manufacturing base has become a draw rather than a risk for Western capital.
Kyiv-based R&D company
Leonardo Ukraine appeared in Ukraine's business register on 20 May, but the company disclosed the step only in its H1 2026 financial report at the end of July. The subsidiary's share capital stands at about $125,000. Leonardo International wholly owns it.
"We have completed the legal process to begin operations. The new company will be used to work in this region," a Leonardo spokesperson said.
The subsidiary will focus on R&D covering communications and navigation systems, software, IT services, and electronic and optical technologies. The step brings Leonardo closer to Ukraine's drone and missile industry, which has expanded rapidly during the war.
Italy wants continental defense alliance, including Ukraine. Kyiv already out-produces all of NATO on drones
From no factory to a Kyiv office
Just over a year ago, then-CEO Roberto Cingolani said that Leonardo had no plans to open a factory in Ukraine, as Reuters reported. At the same time, Cingolani pledged to test Leonardo's Michelangelo Dome air defense system in Ukraine. The Italian government did not reappoint him in April 2026. Lorenzo Mariani took over as CEO in May.
The subsidiary is not a factory. But it gives Mariani a registered legal presence inside Ukraine's defense innovation ecosystem, positioned near the drone and electronic warfare sectors Leonardo wants to tap.
Leonardo is not the first major European defense firm to set up inside Ukraine. Germany's Quantum Systems established three joint ventures and made the country its second-largest international base. Rheinmetall is building an ammunition plant there. Ukrainian defense companies, in turn, have opened production facilities across Europe.

articles.title: Russian drones hit border crossing with Moldova in overnight strike, Ukraine says
articles.body:
The announcement comes a day after a Romanian F-16 fighter jet destroyed an explosive-laden maritime drone close to Europe's largest offshore gas project.
A border crossing with Moldova in Ukraine’s southern Odesa region was damaged by Russian drones overnight, the State Border Guard Service of Ukraine said in a statement on Friday morning.
Traffic through the Tabaky checkpoint has been suspended and diverted to other crossings, the border service said on Telegram.
Moldovan authorities in Chișinău have been informed, the statement added.
The announcement comes a day after a Romanian F-16 fighter jet destroyed an explosive-laden maritime drone close to Europe's largest offshore gas project, hours after another drone entered the NATO member's airspace and crashed near the Ukrainian border.
Romania's President Nicuşor Dan blamed Russia for the latest incident and condemned what he called an escalation of "irresponsible incidents" by Moscow.
Two Romanian F-16 fighter jets were scrambled and one destroyed the drone after authorities decided it posed a potential threat to the hundreds of people working at the site and to critical energy infrastructure.
Defence Minister Radu Miruță said the drone was carrying explosives and that Kyiv had confirmed it was not Ukrainian.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen described the incident as part of "an escalating campaign of threats" against the European Union.
"This is hybrid warfare," she said, accusing those responsible of seeking to unsettle European citizens and divide the bloc.
High alert
Europe as a whole is on high alert after drone flyovers into NATO airspace reached an unprecedented scale last September, prompting European leaders to agree to develop a "drone wall" along their borders to better detect, track and intercept drones violating Europe's airspace.
In November, NATO military officials said a new US anti-drone system had been deployed to the alliance’s eastern flank.
And following a violation of Polish airspace, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte announced the formation of the Eastern Sentry programme, which aims to deter further Russian incursions.
Some European officials described the incidents as Moscow testing NATO’s response, which raised questions about how prepared the alliance is against potential threats from Russia.
The Kremlin has dismissed allegations that Russia is behind some of the unidentified drone flights in Europe as "unfounded."

The frigate’s Trebovaniye-M combat information and control system was also damaged.
Admiral Makarov, the flagship of Russia’s Black Sea Fleet, was reportedly struck in the area of its vertical launch systems. According to the analysis, the impact caused an internal detonation and burned out the ship’s 3S14 launch cells.
The frigate also sustained damage to its radar, electronic warfare, and communications systems.
If the reported damage is confirmed, Russia’s Black Sea Fleet may have lost the operational use of two of its principal Kalibr missile carriers, the outlet reported.
Both vessels could also require extensive repairs if the damage to their launch systems is confirmed, with their return to combat service potentially taking at least a year, according to the assessment.
On August 12, Ukrainian forces launched an overnight strike against Russia’s naval base in Novorossiysk, targeting air defense positions, port berths, and other naval infrastructure, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Zelenskyy described the operation as unique, noting that Novorossiysk serves as Russia’s last major naval stronghold in the Black Sea and lies more than 300 kilometers from the frontline.

articles.title: A suspected Russian intruder in Finland’s sky, and Helsinki wants answers
articles.body:
Finland is investigating a suspected violation of its airspace by a Russian aircraft over the Gulf of Finland, its Defense Ministry said. Authorities have not identified the aircraft or said whether the crossing was deliberate, and the country's border guard has opened an inquiry. The case adds Finland to a growing list of NATO states reporting Russian intrusions along the alliance's frontiers.
What Finland reported
A Russian aircraft is suspected of violating Finnish airspace in the western Gulf of Finland on the afternoon of 20 August, Defense Minister Antti Häkkänen said. He said the country treats every such case seriously and that an inquiry is running.
"Every suspected territorial violation is taken seriously. An investigation is underway," Häkkänen said.
The ministry statement did not name the aircraft. The Border Guard later identified it as a Russian Il-20 reconnaissance plane, Finnish broadcaster Yle reported, saying the suspected crossing lasted about three minutes and reached some 4.7 nautical miles into Finnish airspace at its deepest. It said it would release more as the inquiry advances.
Finland already builds drones with a Ukrainian partner. Joining the drone coalition is the next step
A pattern along NATO's frontiers
The suspected crossing follows two earlier Finnish cases this year. Finland suspected Russian military aircraft of entering its airspace in May, off Porkkala while one avoided a thunderstorm, and again in June, summoning Russia's chargé d'affaires over the two incidents.
Other members of the alliance keep logging similar incidents. Romania has destroyed a sea drone and recovered aerial-drone debris on its soil, and Russian drones have struck near Moldova's border with Ukraine. Kyiv has also accused Russia of steering Ukrainian drones toward Finland and the Baltic States through electronic warfare.
Finland joined NATO in 2023 and has since rearmed sharply, ending a domestic ban on nuclear weapons as part of a wider defense shift. It has stepped up support for Ukraine, most recently backing a power-plant project before Russia's winter energy campaign. Helsinki has also argued it is too early to negotiate with Moscow while the war continues.

articles.title: Israel unleashes new strikes on southern Lebanon (VIDEOS)

Israel unleashes new strikes on southern Lebanon (VIDEOS)
Israeli warplanes carried out a new wave of strikes around Nabatieh, a major city and administrative hub in southern Lebanon, early on Friday, with footage showing powerful explosions lighting up the night sky.
The attacks come despite a US-brokered framework agreed in June aimed at ending fighting between Israel and Hezbollah, the Iran-backed Lebanese armed group. The deal envisages a progressive Israeli withdrawal alongside Lebanese Army deployments and Hezbollah’s disarmament but has stalled over which should come first.
🚨🇱🇧 🇮🇱 Israeli airstrikes are hitting Kfar Rumman alongside the Ali al-Taher Heights

The overnight strikes targeted the town of Kfar Rumman on the outskirts of Nabatieh and the nearby Ali al-Taher Heights, according to Lebanese media. Israeli artillery also struck several other locations across the south.

The Ali al-Taher Heights, which overlook the Nabatieh region and roads leading into the city, have emerged as a focal point of Israel’s military campaign. The Israeli military claims Hezbollah maintains underground infrastructure in the area and has repeatedly targeted the heights in recent weeks.
The latest bombardment comes less than a week after one of the deadliest Israeli attacks in Lebanon since fighting subsided under a June truce. Eleven people were killed in attacks in the south on August 15, according to Lebanese officials. Israel said it was targeting Hezbollah infrastructure.
The attacks come five months after an RT crew was nearly killed while reporting on Israeli operations in the same broader region of southern Lebanon.
RT correspondent Steve Sweeney recently returned with DD Geopolitics reporter Christopher Helali to the damaged Qasmiyeh Bridge over the Litani River, where he and cameraman Ali Rida Sbeity were wounded in an Israeli airstrike on March 19. The conflict in Lebanon is closely tied to Israel’s confrontation with Iran. Hezbollah, Tehran’s longtime ally, resumed attacks on Israel in March following the killing of Iran’s supreme leader, prompting a major Israeli air and ground campaign. Fighting subsided following the Israel-Lebanon truce in June, but Israeli strikes have continued.
Lebanon has condemned the attacks and demanded that Israel withdraw from its territory. Prime Minister Nawaf Salam called last week’s deadly strikes “extremely dangerous” and said any Hezbollah military infrastructure on Lebanese soil should be dealt with by the Lebanese state, not Israel.

articles.title: Former Ukrainian troops tell RT why they chose to fight for Russia
articles.body:
Former Ukrainian troops tell RT why they chose to fight for Russia
Former Ukrainian servicemen switch to the Russian side once they get out of the “information bubble” set up by Vladimir Zelensky’s government and see the reality of the conflict for themselves, a high-ranking officer from a unit comprised of ex-Kiev troops has said.
Earlier in August, Russia announced the creation of the Ukrainian Volunteer Brigade out of several smaller formations of Ukrainian nationals who left the ranks of Kiev’s forces and are now fighting for Russia.
In its report on Thursday, RT Russian shared the stories of some members of the newly-formed brigade.
Some decided to join Russian troops because they changed their views after being captured, some because they never wanted to be in the Ukrainian military, but were forcefully mobilized, and others because they supported Moscow from the start.
The Ukrainian Volunteer Brigade will perform different tasks on the front line. It includes reconnaissance units, an FPV-drone strike squad, and teams handling the evacuation of civilians, among other kinds of troops, the report read.
Highly-motivated troops
A fighter with the callsign ‘Zhak’, who serves as deputy commander for political affairs at the separate battalion ‘Maksim Krivonos’, which also joined the brigade, told RT that the soldiers in his unit have high morale.
“If those people simply didn’t want to fight, they could’ve gone to the detention center after being captured, sit there safe and warm, eat three times a day and wait to be exchanged in a prisoner swap,” said the officer, who was born in Ukraine’s Kharkov Region but has been fighting for Donbass since the Western-backed coup in Kiev in 2014.
The people “in Ukraine… live in a very harsh, aggressive information bubble. But when they find themselves here [in Donbass], when they see the Alley of Angels in Donetsk – they see a completely different picture, and a lot changes in their minds,” Zhak explained.
The Alley of Angels is a monument to hundreds of children killed in Ukrainian attacks on Donbass over the past 12 years.
Our own command ‘wanted to destroy us’
Another member of the brigade, called ‘Hunter’, said that he used to be a research fellow at an agricultural academy in Kiev and was never interested in politics. He was recruited into the Ukrainian military in 2023 after his request for a draft deferment to finish his PhD was denied, he said.
According to Hunter, his company was tasked with controlling “a rather pointless” position in a wooded area that was under constant Russian shelling. When the size of the unit fell from more than a hundred to 20 and then 13 troops, he asked his commanders to order a retreat, but was told to stay put and await reinforcements.
But after a week, no additional troops had arrived. Hunter and his fellow servicemen decided to surrender as soon as Russian forces began storming their trenches.
However, when they left their positions with their hands in the air, the Ukrainian military started firing at them, Hunter noted. “Artillery, mortars and kamikaze-drones were deployed. They didn’t even spare cluster munitions, which surprised me greatly. Our own command wanted to destroy us,” he said.
Hunter stressed that only he and three other troops from the company were lucky enough to survive, with one of them now also fighting for Russia together with him.
‘Patriotism ran out’
Another soldier of the Ukrainian Volunteer Brigade, nicknamed ‘Bely’, told RT that he served as a paratrooper in Kiev’s military and used to be a passionate patriot of Ukraine, despite being born in Donbass. When Ukraine sent its armed forces to the east of the country in 2014, he abandoned his home in what is now Russia’s Lugansk People’s Republic, leaving his wife and son behind, and moved to the city of Dnepropetrovsk (Dnepr), he said.
According to Bely, his marriage fell apart because his spouse was pro-Russian and wanted him to join the self-defense forces in Donbass. But instead he signed another contract with the Ukrainian military in 2016, fighting against the units of the Lugansk and Donetsk People’s Republics.
Despite good pay, “my patriotism ran out, at some point, and the realization began to dawn on me that two brotherly nations were fighting,” the soldier recalled. He was especially impacted by an incident in which Ukraine shelled a school in a village near the city of Lugansk, he added.
Bely said he then lost the will to serve, but the Ukrainian Army refused to discharge him after the escalation between Moscow and Kiev in February 2022. When he surrendered to the Russian military in 2023, he was also targeted by fellow Ukrainian troops, suffering shrapnel wounds, the serviceman said.
Russian medics patched him up, and the experienced soldier was invited to join the Maksim Krivonos battalion while in detention. Bely said he initially had concerns about becoming a traitor to his former Ukrainian comrades-in-arms, but eventually came to the conclusion that fighting for Russia was the right thing to do.

articles.title: Weapons cache linked to Russia reportedly found near Berlin
articles.body:
Weapons cache linked to Russia reportedly found near Berlin
German media outlets have reported that the security services have discovered a secret weapons cache near Berlin which is believed to have been set up on the orders of the Russian secret services.
Source: European Pravda, citing reporting by NDR and WDR, regional public broadcasters, and the newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung
Details: According to the media reports, at the end of last summer security officials received information about a professionally set-up hiding place in Brandenburg, which borders the capital Berlin, and found two pistols there.
Germany's domestic intelligence agency, the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV), believes the forest hideout was set up on the orders of the Russian secret services.
The Federal Prosecutor's Office is conducting an investigation, acting on the suspicion that a serious act of violence endangering the state was being plotted. A suspect has been detained in Romania.
The media reported that the weapons found had been disabled, and the cache was placed under surveillance, but this yielded no results. Media reports suggest the perpetrators likely realised they had been exposed.
The German security services are now convinced the weapons were being stored for agents who intended to carry out "kinetic operations" on Moscow's behalf in Germany, including assassinations.
Sinan Selen, President of the BfV, has been warning for several months that Russia could carry out attacks against specific individuals. The potential targets named include weapons manufacturers, exiled opposition figures and supporters of Ukraine.
Background:
- Earlier, Stefan Thumann, CEO of the German drone manufacturer Donaustahl, said he had been forced into hiding from the Russian secret services amid reports of an assassination plot.
- In the summer of 2024, CNN reported a foiled attempt by Russian secret services to kill Armin Papperger, CEO of German arms manufacturer Rheinmetall.
- In January 2025, NATO officially confirmed that Russia had intended to kill Papperger.

articles.title: Ukrainian Drones Hit Major Lukoil Refinery, Military Airfield as Russia Claims 325 UAVs Downed
articles.body:
Ukrainian drones struck Russia’s Perm Krai on the morning of Aug. 21, with eyewitness footage indicating that the Lukoil-Permnefteorgsintez oil refinery was targeted and a large fire broke out at the facility.
The regional Ministry of Territorial Security declared a drone alert that lasted for more than two hours. Russia’s Federal Air Transporta Agency, Rosaviatsiya, also restricted arrivals and departures at Perm’s Bolshoye Savino Airport.
Residents reported several explosions and a large plume of smoke over the city.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
According to the Russian independent outlet Astra, which analyzed eyewitness footage, the apparent target was the Lukoil-Permnefteorgsintez (PNOS) refinery.
The refinery is among Russia’s 10 largest oil-processing facilities and is Lukoil’s second-largest refinery after its facility in Nizhny Novgorod.
In 2024, PNOS processed 12.6 million metric tons of crude oil, including approximately 2 million tons of gasoline and 5.3 million tons of diesel fuel.
The refinery produces a range of petroleum products, including gasoline, diesel, aviation fuel and lubricants. It is a major industrial facility in the region and supplies both Russia’s domestic market and foreign markets.
President Volodymyr Zelensky later confirmed that Ukrainian drones struck an oil refinery in Perm overnight.
“We continue to use our long-range sanctions to return the consequences of the war to where it came from,” he wrote.
Nord Stream Suspect Arrested on Set of Film About the Sabotage
According to Zelensky, the target was located more than 1,600 kilometers (994 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
The Ukrainian General Staff added that the strikes sparked a fire at the Perm refinery.
“The plant refines oil and produces more than 60 types of products. The depth of oil refining is about 98%, one of the highest among Russian oil refineries. The enterprise is involved in supplying the Russian army,” the General Staff said.
The General Staff also reported that a second target was the Marynovka military airfield in Russia’s Volgograd region. The extent of the damage there is still being assessed.
Zelensky also provided details on the results of earlier Ukrainian strikes.
A Russian Su-34 fighter-bomber was damaged at the Akhtubinsk airfield, located about 600 kilometers (373 miles) from the front line.
In Primorsko-Akhtarsk, about 180 kilometers (112 miles) from the front line, Ukrainian forces struck a facility used to store, prepare and launch attack drones that Russia uses to strike Ukraine.
“I thank all units of the Defense Forces of Ukraine for their accuracy and precision. Glory to Ukraine!” Zelensky added.
Refinery repeatedly targeted
The Perm refinery was targeted by drones less than a month ago, on July 29, when a fire also broke out at the facility. The AVT-5 crude oil refining unit was reportedly damaged in that attack.
The plant was also targeted on May 7 and April 30, with drone attacks reportedly disrupting its operations and forcing it to halt fuel production on several occasions.
The latest strike came as Ukrainian forces continued to target Russia’s oil-refining infrastructure.
On Aug. 20, Ukrainian drones attacked the Taneco refinery in Tatarstan for the second time in two weeks. A week earlier, the Gazpromneftekhim Salavat refinery in Bashkortostan was also targeted.
Industry sources previously told Reuters that at least four Russian refineries had stopped processing crude oil since early August following drone attacks. The affected facilities included the Orsknefteorgsintez refinery in Orenburg Oblast, the Zapsibneftekhim refinery in Tyumen Oblast, and the Saratov and Volgograd refineries.
Russia reports 325 Ukrainian drones downed
Russia’s Defense Ministry claimed that its air defenses shot down 325 Ukrainian drones overnight.
According to the ministry, the drones were intercepted over the Astrakhan, Belgorod, Bryansk, Volgograd, Voronezh, Kaluga, Kursk, Oryol, Rostov, Ryazan and Tula regions, as well as Moscow Oblast, the annexed Crimean Peninsula, Udmurtia, Krasnodar Krai and Perm Krai.
It also reported interceptions over the waters of the Azov and Black seas.
The Russian Defense Ministry’s figures could not be independently verified.

articles.title: Ukraine’s biggest weakness against Russia isn’t interceptor shortage, analyst argues. It’s what happens before missiles even launch
articles.body:
Ukraine’s failure to anticipate and prepare for Russian threats is a bigger problem than the shortage of air defenses, says Oleksandr Kovalenko of the Information Resistance group. Russia, meanwhile, has demonstrated its ability to develop and execute medium-term plans for terror operations that can take years to prepare, according to Obozrevatel.
Russian forces adapt almost every month to new challenges and opportunities, scaling up their attacks. The use of jet-powered Banderol drone missiles is one example.
Russia is now employing a “tactical adaptive distribution” approach, flexibly redirecting missiles and strike drones toward different regions and rear cities depending on Ukrainian air-defense capabilities.
The main difference
The key change in Russia’s 2026 campaign against Ukraine’s rear areas has been the growing use of jet-powered drones based on the Iranian Shahed-238 and Karrar, which Russia has localized as Geran-3/4/5.
Russia first used a jet-powered kamikaze drone against Ukraine in January 2024. These weapons have been continuously upgraded over the past two years.
Ukraine, however, failed to adequately anticipate the threat and now lacks an effective, low-cost way to intercept Geran-3/4/5 drones, Kovalenko says. Russian forces used more than 1,400 jet-powered drones in the first half of 2026 alone, compared with 180 throughout all of 2025.
“It is possible that the facility in Alabuga, Tatarstan, could eventually be fully converted to producing jet-powered kamikaze drones as part of this strategy,” the analyst said.
What comes next: strikes on Kyiv to exert psychological pressure
A significant share of Russia’s new hard-to-intercept weapon variants appears to be concentrated for strikes on Kyiv.
Russian forces are seeking to exploit Ukraine’s acute shortage of Patriot and SAMP/T interceptors, using the opportunity to intensify their campaign of terror. Russia has previously used similar tactics to exert psychological pressure on civilians and disrupt economic activity in regions including Kharkiv and Odesa.
The same approach could increasingly be directed at the capital, particularly ahead of and during Ukraine’s Independence Day.

articles.title: What is Egypt's role in the new regional security order?
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
What is Egypt's role in the new regional security order?
Egypt's current absence from the collective security pact signed between Turkey, Pakistan, and Saudi Arabia, dubbed the ‘Mecca Agreement’, has brought renewed attention to Egypt’s security strategy towards its regional allies and the wider region.
While speculation surrounding Egypt’s absence from the agreement abounds, understanding Cairo’s position requires looking beyond the Mecca Agreement.
Egypt’s regional security posture has historically been shaped by a preference for strategic flexibility, driven by the recognition that its interests often require maintaining relationships with competing regional and international actors.
Today, this approach is being tested by an increasingly volatile regional environment marked by state and non-state threats, from Israel’s expanding regional wars to the US-Israel-Iran war and its fallout.
The complexities of this geostrategic environment have compelled Cairo to emphasise diplomacy, mediation, and issue-based security cooperation over concrete, bloc-based alignments.
Its rapprochement with Turkey, expanding security ties with major regional players including Saudi Arabia, and maintenance of diplomatic backchannels with rival actors underscore Egypt’s efforts to diversify its security partnerships while preserving the flexibility to engage across regional fault lines.
Security through diplomacy
A 1955 telegram from the US Embassy in Cairo to the US Department of State documented a tense exchange between then Egyptian President Gamal Abdel Nasser and then US Assistant Secretary of State George Allen over Egypt’s acquisition of Czechoslovak arms.
During the exchange, Nasser expressed doubts about Washington’s reliability as a security partner and raised concerns about Israel’s growing influence and territorial ambitions, particularly the influence of the Herut party, the predecessor to today’s Likud.
The exchange reflects a key feature of Egyptian strategic thinking. Cairo has long been sceptical of overreliance on a single external security umbrella, preferring instead to preserve room for manoeuvre.
That instinct remains salient in Cairo’s approach today. "Egypt has largely focused on managing and balancing its bilateral relationships with all major regional players to address growing instability and threats,” Liam Karr, Africa Team Lead at the Critical Threats Project, told The New Arab.
Egypt’s security is increasingly being tested by instability beyond its immediate borders, primarily driven by Israel’s expanding regional wars and now compounded by the US-Israel-Iran war. Previously assumed to be relatively shielded from these developments, Egypt has increasingly found itself directly exposed to their consequences.
Israel’s war on Gaza heightened Egyptian threat perceptions, particularly amid Israeli calls at the time for the displacement of Palestinians into Sinai, a scenario Cairo repeatedly identified as a red line.
The war also brought Israeli incursions closer to Egyptian territory. Throughout the war, Israel repeatedly asserted control over the Philadelphi Corridor, a narrow strip along the Egypt-Gaza border whose security arrangements have been shaped by the 1979 Egypt-Israel Peace Treaty and subsequent agreements.
“Egypt’s threat perception has been shaped particularly by Israel’s unilateral security expansionism. This perception led to a greater emphasis on mediation across regional fault lines, while balancing against Cairo’s rivals, first and foremost Israel,” Ahmed Aboudouh, Associate Fellow at Chatham House’s Middle East and North Africa Programme, told The New Arab.
Egypt’s response focused heavily on diplomacy. Alongside Qatar, Cairo maintained a central role in efforts to mediate between Israel and Hamas, positioning itself as an intermediary capable of communicating with multiple sides.
Earlier this month, US special envoy Jared Kushner met a Hamas delegation led by Khalil al-Hayya in Egypt, in a rare direct high-level meeting, to discuss implementation of the Board of Peace’s roadmap, namely the question of Hamas’s disarmament.
A durable end to the war on Gaza is vital to Egypt’s economic and security stability, particularly as the conflict continues to generate pressure along its border and across the Red Sea. Egypt’s economic vulnerabilities have raised the stakes. The Suez Canal, one of the country’s main sources of foreign currency, saw revenues collapse by roughly two-thirds at the height of Houthi attacks on Red Sea shipping.
The resumption of attacks on Red Sea shipping and rising regional tensions stemming from the US-Israel-Iran war further jeopardise Egypt’s economic security. Cairo also remains heavily reliant on Gulf investment and financial support, making stability across the Gulf and Red Sea increasingly inseparable from its own economic security.
The Egyptian economy has, however, shown some signs of recovery. In July, the IMF reinforced confidence in Egypt’s economic reform program, unlocking an additional $1.8 billion in funds after Cairo completed its latest review. That said, underlying vulnerabilities remain.
The widening geography of the US-Israel-Iran war was underscored in late July, when a drone struck Egypt’s Damietta port. The incident marked the first attack on Egyptian territory since the outbreak of the war, illustrating the interconnectedness of regional conflicts and directly exposing Egypt to new security threats. It also highlighted the urgency of reaching a durable resolution.
Egypt’s diplomatic leverage derives in large part from its ability to maintain relationships across divides. Earlier this year, Egypt used its diplomatic backchannel with the IRGC, an increasingly prominent decision-making actor in Iran, to help preserve a line of contact during a moment of heightened tension. Given the trajectory of regional dynamics, these channels are likely to remain important.
Egypt has also demonstrated a willingness to extend military support to its regional partners. During Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El Sisi’s visit to Abu Dhabi in May, he visited an Egyptian fighter detachment stationed in the UAE comprising Rafale jets and Egyptian pilots, alongside reports of Egyptian defensive deployments in Saudi Arabia.
Gulf security is closely aligned with Egyptian interests, but Cairo’s current absence from the Mecca agreement may reflect a recognition of the risks that a more hardened posture could invite, as well as a preference for maintaining strategic balance.
Issue-based cooperation over bloc alignment
Egypt maintains robust security relationships with all three members of the Mecca Agreement. Its current absence from the pact should therefore not be interpreted as a rejection of closer regional security cooperation.
Egypt and Turkey have considerably expanded their security cooperation as part of their broader political rapprochement. In June, the two countries conducted joint F-16 drills, the first exercise of its kind in almost two decades, building on the momentum generated by their 2025 joint maritime exercise, “Sea of Friendship.”
Ankara and Cairo have also pledged greater coordination on regional files including Sudan, Libya, and Gaza. Additionally, defence-industrial cooperation has expanded. Ankara and Cairo signed agreements worth approximately $350 million earlier this year aimed primarily at expanding joint production efforts.
These initiatives serve Egypt’s immediate defence needs while simultaneously enhancing regional strategic autonomy.
Cairo’s relationship with Riyadh is similarly deep. Egypt was among the 14 founding members of the Saudi-led Red Sea security maritime force. Its participation also builds on extensive experience in collective maritime security initiatives, including its current command, for the second time, of the Combined Maritime Forces’ Combined Task Force-153, the Red Sea focused task force.
“Egypt wants to be a central leader to regional approaches in its backyard, as shown by its involvement in the Sudan Quad, various multilateral security initiatives in the Red Sea, and the Libya and Palestine peace processes,” Karr told The New Arab.
Diversified partnerships
Participation in a formal collective security pact could strengthen deterrence, but it could also narrow Egypt’s room for manoeuvre and constrain its ability to mediate across regional divides.
“Egypt will maintain its cautious, defensive and risk-averse approach to avoid antagonising any party with leverage to pressure its direct national interests,” said Aboudouh.
Egypt will likely continue diversifying its security partnerships rather than committing to formal blocs. In line with this posture, China and Egypt are currently hosting the second iteration of their joint aerial exercise, "Eagles of Civilisation," from mid-August to early September, following the inaugural exercise held in 2025.
Strategically, Cairo will also have to guard against military overstretch as it manages simultaneous pressure across two turbulent fronts, the Middle East and the Nile Basin. Ethiopia's plans for three additional dams on the Nile have already drawn strong opposition from Cairo.
Managing these competing pressures will reinforce Egypt’s preference for diversified partnerships and strategic flexibility, allowing it to deepen cooperation where its interests converge while avoiding overreliance on any single security partner.
Hana Elshehaby is a Senior Research Assistant for the Middle East Council on Global Affairs. She is also a Non-Resident Fellow at the Institute for Middle East Options

articles.title: Air defense downs 107 of 135 Russia targets; 27 strike UAVs hit 16 locations
articles.body:
Ukraine’s Defense Forces intercepted 107 Russia targets overnight into Friday; however, hits by 27 strike UAVs were recorded across 16 locations, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported.
"According to preliminary data, as of 08:00, air defense shot down/neutralized 107 Russia UAVs of the Shahed type, Gerber, and other drone types in the north, south, and east of the country," the statement said.
In total, on the night of August 21 (from 18:00 on August 20), Russia attacked with 135 strike UAVs of the Shahed type (including jet-powered variants), Gerbera, and "Parodiya" decoy drones from the directions of Kursk, Millerovo, Orel, Primorsko-Akhtarsk (Russia), occupied Donetsk, and occupied AR Crimea.

articles.title: Simultaneous Russian attack on NATO and Chinese operation in Taiwan would be very dangerous scenario - Dolhov
articles.body:
Simultaneous Russian attack on NATO and Chinese operation in Taiwan would be very dangerous scenario - Dolhov
At the same time, one of the most dangerous potential scenarios is the simultaneous outbreak of two large-scale crises—a Russian attack against a NATO member state and a Chinese operation against Taiwan. Ukrainian diplomat Ihor Dolhov expressed this view in his program “Ihor Dolhov’s Program,” which was released on Ukrinform’s YouTube channel.
He noted that Ukraine possesses Patriot anti-aircraft missile launchers but currently faces a shortage of missiles to counter Russian ballistic attacks. According to Dolhov, the problem with stocks of such missiles is not limited to Ukraine. “There are fewer of them in the United States. There are fewer of them in Europe. There are fewer of them in other countries,” the diplomat noted.
Dolhov attributes this situation, in particular, to the extensive use of American weapons during the Gulf War.
At the same time, Russia continues its massive attacks on Ukraine and is striking Ukrainian ports, creating additional risks not only to the country’s security but also to its economy. According to Dolhov, Russian strikes have significantly hampered exports through Black Sea ports, and a further blockade of Ukrainian agricultural exports could have consequences for global food security. “A humanitarian crisis, a food crisis due to a shortage of wheat and grains on the market. Russia is also threatening to freeze Ukraine out this winter,” the diplomat noted.
He emphasized that, at the same time, the international security situation is deteriorating: Russia is escalating its threats against European countries and Japan, while the war in the Middle East is diverting a significant portion of U.S. military resources.
According to Dolhov, this creates additional opportunities for China to increase pressure around Taiwan.
The diplomat cited the simultaneous outbreak of two large-scale crises—a Russian attack against one of the NATO member states and a Chinese operation against Taiwan—as one of the most dangerous potential scenarios. “And NATO will have no means to respond. Nor will the United States be able to help either Europe or Taiwan. They will be completely tied up in the war in the Persian Gulf,” Dolhov stated.
According to him, under such conditions, Europe must focus not only on finding a new format for negotiations but, above all, on strengthening its ability to deter Russia and compel it to engage in genuine negotiations.
Earlier, The Atlantic reported that NATO leadership is taking increasingly seriously the scenario of a simultaneous attack by Russia on Europe and by China on Taiwan. At the same time, the U.S. and NATO are not prepared for a simultaneous war with Russia and China.

articles.title: With ICC sanctions, Trump wants to make the world safe for war criminals | Kenneth Roth
articles.body:
The Trump administration has taken another step in its crusade against the international criminal court by imposing sanctions on two more senior ICC officials. The growing number of sanctioned jurists – now 13 – does not change the lawless nature of this quest.
Donald Trump and his henchman, Marco Rubio, want to make the world safe for US and Israeli war criminals. No one should let them.
The latest victims of Trump’s vendetta are the ICC president – its chief judge, Tomoko Akane of Japan – and Abdoulaye Seye of Senegal, a senior ICC trial lawyer, evidently for his role advancing the prosecution of Israeli officials. Yet the real victims are not these particular individuals, but people worldwide who look to the court as one of the few avenues of recourse against unscrupulous leaders who commit mass atrocities such as fighting wars by targeting civilians.
We should never let Trump normalize these sanctions. Their main effect is to deprive the target of the ability to use the international financial system – no credit cards, no access to banks, extreme difficulty navigating a modern economy. That is a tool once reserved for corrupt or violent officials who were otherwise beyond the law. Trump is using them to attack the public officials who would bring such heinous individuals to justice.
Rubio, the secretary of state, dressed up the sanctions with high-sounding rhetoric about the ICC threatening “America sovereignty”. That is true only if Americans (and Israelis) have a sovereign right to commit war crimes wherever they want. Even Rubio cannot get himself to spell out what King Trump’s campaign is really about.
Rubio’s main articulated complaint is that the ICC can “investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute officials whose government has not consented to ICC jurisdiction”. That is true, but it is wrong only if one adopts a conveniently (for Washington and the Israeli government) narrow sense of how the court should obtain jurisdiction for a crime.
On the one hand, when a country joins the ICC, it accepts the court’s jurisdiction over its citizens. That might be called jurisdiction by virtue of nationality. The US government accepts that route to jurisdiction because it never joined the court.
But when a country becomes a court member, it also confers jurisdiction over crimes on its territory, even when committed by a foreigner. That is hardly controversial. A hallmark of sovereignty is the ability to enforce the law on a country’s own territory. Even the Trump administration would not dare object to, say, the British government prosecuting an American for a crime committed in London.
But the administration claims it is somehow an outrage if a country confers that same territorial jurisdiction on the ICC for war crimes and similar atrocities committed by foreigners on its territory – a major purpose of the court. The US government objected to such territorial jurisdiction when the court’s treaty was adopted at a major diplomatic conference in Rome in 1998 – and lost overwhelmingly, by a vote of 120 to seven.
Since then, even the US government has accepted territorial jurisdiction when convenient. After the ICC used it to prosecute Vladimir Putin (Russia never joined the court) for the kidnapping of children from Ukraine (a member), Joe Biden called the prosecution “justified”. The late senator Lindsey Graham, a Republican leader on foreign policy, orchestrated a unanimous Senate resolution in support.
But for Trump, territorial jurisdiction suddenly became toxic again when it was used to charge Benjamin Netanyahu and the former Israeli defense minister Yoav Gallant with deliberately starving and depriving Palestinian civilians in Gaza. Israel is not a member of the ICC, but Palestine, where the alleged crimes took place, is.
Territorial jurisdiction can also be used to charge foreigners from non-member states with aiding and abetting crimes in a state where the ICC has jurisdiction. For example, the court might charge United Arab Emirates officials with aiding and abetting genocide in the Darfur region of Sudan by sending arms and mercenaries to the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, Rwandan officials with aiding and abetting war crimes in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo by arming and supporting the M23 rebel group, or US officials (Trump’s real concern) with aiding and abetting Israel’s genocide in Gaza by supplying arms and military aid.
Indeed, territorial jurisdiction means that the sanctions themselves could lead to prosecution of Trump and Rubio. Article 70 of the Rome Statute, the ICC’s founding treaty, codifies the crime of obstructing justice when someone retaliates “against an official of the Court on account of duties performed”. That’s exactly what the Trump-Rubio sanctions do. The court would have jurisdiction because the sanctions relate to the prosecution of Israeli officials for crimes committed on Palestinian territory.
Rubio has vowed to dismantle the ICC “brick by brick, if necessary”, announcing: “We expect more countries to join our campaign by ending their funding and participation in this politicized and unaccountable court.” Yet that bombast so far has produced few results among the court’s 125 members.
Venezuela, which has become a US vassal state since Trump’s seizure of Nicolás Maduro, has announced its withdrawal. So has Chad, which announced its departure after a call from a state department official. But Chadian officials have their own reasons to worry about the court because they allowed their territory to be used by the UAE to arm the RSF in Sudan.
(Separately from Trump’s campaign, three military juntas in the Sahel have also announced their exit from the ICC: Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso.)
Yet if the response to the Trump administration’s call to leave the court so far has been tepid, the defense of the court by its supposed closest defenders has not exactly been vigorous. The European Union has what is known as a “blocking statute”, legislation designed to negate the application of US sanctions in Europe by prohibiting European banks from complying. But while the EU says it “deeply regrets” these new sanctions on the ICC, it has not invoked the blocking statute to protect court personnel.
One reason appears to be fear among banks, particularly in the Netherlands, of retaliation from Trump. The ICC is located in the Hague, also the Dutch seat of government.
In other words, as European officials see it, fighting genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity is important. Trump’s efforts to allow Americans and Israelis to commit these crimes with impunity is disgraceful. But if defending the rule of law might put Dutch banks in Trump’s crosshairs, justice can wait.
The EU can do better than that.
- 
  Kenneth Roth is a Guardian US columnist, a senior fellow at Yale University and a former executive director of Human Rights Watch. He is the author of Righting Wrongs: Three Decades on the Front Lines Battling Abusive Governments

articles.title: A biolaboratory complex was created on an island: the Defence Intelligence of Ukraine says that Russia is experimenting with viruses in the middle of a reservoir
articles.body:
A biolaboratory complex was created on an island: the Defence Intelligence of Ukraine says that Russia is experimenting with viruses in the middle of a reservoir
Kyiv • UNN
The Defence Intelligence of Ukraine said that Russia created a secret complex on an island in Tver Oblast for experiments with dangerous pathogens. The intelligence service warned of the risk of contamination of the reservoir and epidemics.
The aggressor state Russia has built a secret military complex of biological laboratories in Tver Oblast, where, under the guise of veterinary and physiological research, it is experimenting with dangerous viruses and other pathogens in the interests of the armed forces, UNN reports, citing the Defence Intelligence of Ukraine.
Details
As reported by the intelligence service, the facility, officially called the "Center for Experimental Physiology," is located on "Lisiy" Island in the middle of the Vyshny Volochyok Reservoir.
Since 2023, the waters around the island with the biological laboratories have been closed to fishing, swimming, and boating as a "specially protected territory of regional significance."
The reservoir supplies fresh water to a number of settlements, including the city of Vyshny Volochyok, and is also the source of the Tvertsa River, which flows into the Volga. If dangerous pathogens or chemicals from the biological laboratories enter the reservoir, the consequences of outbreaks of epidemics and infections could be catastrophic not only for the region's population but for all of Russia, the statement said.
The Defence Intelligence of Ukraine added that the biological laboratory complex project was implemented on the orders of Russian dictator Vladimir Putin as a particularly important facility—intended to "ensure Russia's defense capability and security." Formally, it was incorporated into the structure of the Federal Medical-Biological Agency.
The closed facility on "Lisiy" Island is under enhanced security. The complex is protected from the air by crews operating surface-to-air missile systems. The Kremlin assigned responsibility for the security regime to Defense Minister Andrei Belousov. Soldiers involved in guarding the facility privately express fear of becoming infected with an unknown "filth."
The Defence Intelligence of Ukraine recalled that in the spring of 2026, an epidemic of foot-and-mouth disease among cattle broke out in Russia, which Moscow tried to conceal from the world and its own population. It cannot be ruled out that this and other similar cases may have resulted from unsuccessful Russian experiments with viruses, bacteria, and other pathogens.
Recall
Earlier, the Defence Intelligence of the Ministry of Defence of Ukraine reported that Russian occupiers were creating conditions for the spread of anthrax in the temporarily occupied Ukrainian territories.

articles.title: Russia Unleashes 135 Drones on Ukraine, Killing 2 in Kharkiv Region and Injuring 6 in Sumy
articles.body:
Russian forces launched a massive overnight drone attack on Ukraine, sending 135 Shahed-type and other unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) toward the country and striking civilian areas in Sumy and Kharkiv regions.
In Sumy city, the attack damaged residential buildings and civilian infrastructure and injured six people, including a 16-year-old girl. In the Kharkiv region, two women were killed and two people were injured after Russian drones struck the village of Lebyazhe in the Chuhuiv district.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Drone attack damages homes and infrastructure in Sumy
Russian drones attacked Sumy early on Friday, Aug. 21, causing fires in residential areas and injuring six people, according to Serhii Kryvosheyenko, head of the Sumy City Military Administration (MVA).
The massive UAV attack targeted civilian infrastructure and the residential sector in the city’s Kovpakiv district, Kryvosheyenko said.
One of the strikes caused a fire in a two-story residential building. Fires also broke out at several other locations.
The threat of additional Russian strikes complicated the work of rescuers, according to Kryvosheyenko.
Six people were injured in the attack: a 16-year-old girl, four women aged 36, 39, 50 and 66, and a 35-year-old man. All are receiving medical treatment.
Nine residential buildings were damaged at four locations across the city. Damage included broken windows and balcony frames. A shop, gas-station infrastructure, sections of roadway and several vehicles were also damaged.
Finland suspects Russian plane of violating its airspace
Emergency and recovery crews are continuing to clear the consequences of the attack.
Two killed in Russian drone strike on Kharkiv region
The State Emergency Service (DSNS) reported that two people were killed and two others injured in a separate massive drone attack on the Kharkiv region.
Russian forces overnight targeted the village of Lebyazhe in the Chuhuiv district, striking a residential area.
The attack destroyed and damaged several private homes and sparked a fire covering approximately 400 square meters. Five residential buildings and vehicles caught fire.
Rescuers recovered the bodies of two women from the rubble.
Emergency crews are extinguishing the fire and carrying out search-and-rescue operations. Municipal services and equipment from a local agricultural enterprise are also assisting at the scene.
Ukraine downs 107 Russian drones
According to the Ukrainian Air Force, Russia launched 135 Shahed-type attack drones, including jet-powered variants, as well as Gerber and Parody decoy drones, beginning at 6 p.m. on Aug. 20.
The attack was countered by Ukrainian aviation, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare and unmanned-systems units, as well as mobile fire groups.
As of 8 a.m. Friday, Ukrainian air defenses had shot down or suppressed 107 Russian drones across northern, southern and eastern Ukraine, according to preliminary data.
The Air Force said 27 attack UAVs reached 16 locations, while debris from downed drones fell at three additional sites.

articles.title: MQ-9 Lost in Middle East Last Year Due to Chafed Wire: New Report
articles.body:
A frayed wire likely triggered stray voltage to shut off a fuel valve, causing the catastrophic loss of an MQ-9 Reaper drone last August, according to a new Air Force investigation report.
The aircraft, valued at $23.6 million, was destroyed in place. It is among at least 40 MQ-9s lost or shot down over the past 18 months.
Air Combat Command released the Accident Investigation Board report on Aug. 13, nearly a year after the Aug. 31, 2025, mishap. The exact location of the mishap was not disclosed—the report said only that it took place in the U.S. Central Command area of responsibility.
The MQ-9 belonged to the 432nd Wing at Creech Air Force Base, Nev., while the pilot and sensor operator were from the 89th Attack Squadron at Ellsworth Air Force Base, S.D. The drone was returning from a mission to its base in the region and had been in the air nearly 19 hours when the engine shut off.
The drone automatically attempted to restart the twice, and the crew tried two manual restarts as well before the Reaper crashed to the ground. Operators tried for a soft landing to preserve the aircraft but were not successful.
After sorting through several options to avoid population centers and minimize damage, the crew selected a “relatively flat and isolated” piece of desert and tried to go in with the landing gear down, according to the report. But the crew lost contact with the aircraft as it descended below 2,000 feet.
The Reaper landed near the selected landing area, but “the force of the impact caused its landing gear to collapse,” according to the report. “Following the landing, sensitive equipment was removed from the [aircraft] and the remaining wreckage was demolished on site.”
The problem occurred on the aircraft’s first flight after its engine was replaced as part of a routine 3,000-hour engine inspection. During that inspection, personnel from contractor Honeywell noted three issues beyond normal wear:
- The propeller governor cable was chafed and replaced
- The fuel control unit was replaced with a new unit overhauled in April 2025, due to a missing log card
- The compressor seal was leaking and replaced
Notably, the inspection and replacement routine did not include removing the top cover from the fuel control unit, which regulates the flow of fuel to the engine—despite “known examples of the FCU sensor wire chafing,” according to MQ-9 manufacturer General Atomics. Honeywell personnel reported they had observed “a relay wire shorting and sparking” while servicing a different aircraft.
Based on data logs, investigators determined the MQ-9 engine experienced a spike in fuel flow just before plummeting to zero. General Atomics was able to recreate that sequence in its lab by suddenly closing the electrical fuel shutoff valve.
Those tests, combined with the known issue of the wires chafing inside the fuel control unit, led investigators to conclude the most likely explanation for the mishap was that a frayed wire inside the fuel control unit leaked enough voltage to trigger the fuel shutoff valve to close.
The board noted that while most U.S. Air Force aircraft are required to undergo some sort of check flight after their engine is replaced “to ensure the aircraft is airworthy and to test the flight integrity of all systems, particularly critical systems like those affecting engines,” the MQ-9 maintenance manual has no such requirement, the board said.
What’s more, investigators noted with surprise that a complete engine change is considered “routine maintenance” on MQ-9s, and that the crew controlling the drone was never informed that their aircraft had just received an entirely new engine.
The Accident Investigation Board cited inadequate planning and briefing and inadequate written standards as “relevant factors” in the mishap.
MQ-9 Losses
The MQ-9 mishap occurred during a relative lull in operations in the Middle East. Just months earlier, from March to May 2025, Operation Rough Rider sought to halt attacks on commercial shipping by Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen. The Houthis downed about a half dozen MQ-9s during that stretch using electro-optical/infrared surface-to-air missile systems, Air & Space Forces Magazine previously reported.
At least two dozen MQ-9s were subsequently lost during Operation Epic Fury against Iran starting in late February, some to air defense missiles and some struck on the ground.
By May, after a brief ceasefire took hold, the Air Force was down around 30 Reapers, Air & Space Forces Magazine reported. Hostilities began again in earnest by July, and the Washington Post reported last week that “at least 45” MQ-9s have been destroyed.
The Air Force reported having 230 MQ-9s in its inventory at the start of fiscal 2025; one year later, it had just 182. In May, Lt. Gen. David Tabor, Air Force deputy chief of staff for plans and programs, said the fleet was down to around 135 aircraft.
Air Force officials have praised the performance of the MQ-9 in the Iran conflict, saying it has accounted for many of the thousands of strikes conducted during the campaign and gathered valuable intelligence. Some have also hinted that commanders have sometimes employed them in ways that put the drones at greater risk.
With the fleet shrinking, leaders are discussing how to replace the losses. Options include acquiring the few remaining MQ-9As from General Atomics, buying the larger MQ-9Bs now being built, or developing replacement platforms. Among the alternatives backed by some on the Air Staff is a project jointly pursued by the Defense Innovation Unit and the Air Force. The so-called “massed modular aircraft,” or MMA is conceived as an “attritable” aircraft whose loss is treated more like a munition than a aircraft. Vendors have offered proposals and an acquisition official said in July that one or competitors could be selected by the end of 2026.

articles.title: ‘I don’t think beyond tomorrow’: How people in occupied Crimea are surviving one of the hardest summers of the war
articles.body:
‘I don’t think beyond tomorrow’: How people in occupied Crimea are surviving one of the hardest summers of the war
This summer in occupied Crimea has been one of the hardest in decades: Crimean cities are regularly shelled by Ukraine, there are few tourists, prices are rising, and there are regular outages of electricity, water, and gasoline. The Bereg cooperative talked to Crimean residents living in different parts of the region, from Dzhankoi to Alupka, about how they’re surviving and why they don’t even consider leaving. Meduza is publishing this piece in full.
The names of the people in this story have been changed for their safety.
‘We live like this: we buy a piece of meat at the store, cook it right away, and eat it’
Iryna
Dzhankoi; about 40 kilometers (25 miles) from mainland Ukraine
I’m from the Kherson region, but I moved to Dzhankoi in 2023. I don’t have any relatives here. We [my husband and I and our two children] moved on our own. We live in a two-story house in Dzhankoi, and when there are strikes, we go down from the second floor and sit in the bathroom.
Strikes happen regularly here. Drones target electrical substations and are shot down right over residential neighborhoods. In May, one hit a house, killing five people, damaging nearby buildings, including stores, and blowing out windows and doors. Since then, drones have also struck the railway station and a substation. Coming from the Kherson region, though, I’ve long since gotten used to all this.
We had no power for two weeks starting July 6. Now it’s back for four hours a day, at just 95 volts — not enough to run a refrigerator or washing machine. The only thing we can manage is charging a phone. We live like this: we buy a piece of meat at the store and cook and eat it right away. It’s not like before, when the refrigerator was always full. And now we wash our clothes by hand.
Authorities promised a [one-time] payment of 15,000 rubles per person to anyone who went without power for more than 48 hours. I applied on July 12, and it’s still under review, even though I’ve seen reports that other people have already been paid.
My older child used to go to daycare, but it closed for two weeks of repairs at the start of summer. It was supposed to reopen on July 1 but never did — all the daycares are now closed because of the power situation. Only emergency programs remain open, for children whose parents work and have no one else to watch them.
We bought an inverter generator for 25,000 rubles, which we turn on in the evening so our son can watch cartoons for a couple of hours. Our daughter, who’s a year old, is afraid of the dark, so turn on a lamp for her before bed to help calm her fears.
Water runs from 6 p.m. to 10 a.m., but the pressure is too weak to wash properly. It’s only strong enough at 3 a.m., so that’s when you wash your hair.
Gas right now [August 10] costs 190 rubles for 95 octane and 150 rubles for 92 octane, though it’s also sold for as much as 300 rubles, with lines stretching for kilometers. My family doesn’t have a car, but I know the going rate because a friend of mine paid that price.
Every product is still available in stores, but prices have risen sharply for staples like bread, sunflower oil, and sugar. A kilogram [2.2 pounds] of sugar used to cost 70 rubles; now it’s 100. Supermarkets bought powerful generators so shoppers could still get butter, sausage, and cheese, and customers can charge phones and power banks inside — the same goes for the city administration building and the local history museum. Walk down the street now and you’ll hear an incredible noise from all the generators.
I’m on maternity leave, and my husband used to work as a freight forwarder, but the company shut down until September. People think everything will get better in the fall, but I wonder what exactly they expect to change come September. Nobody really knows.
In any case, my husband found another job and is now doing an internship. Work is hard to find right now — the Dzhankoi dairy plant and several other companies have closed — and some of our acquaintances are simply staying home.
We’re planning to stay in Dzhankoi — I don’t see the point in fleeing somewhere else, since even a place like Krasnodar gets hit too. What makes me angriest is that the [city] administration isn’t doing anything about the power, while in Krasnoperekopsk, Armiansk, and Krasnohvardiiske, everything has already been fixed and the power is back on. We’re told the electricians are working around the clock, but I don’t believe it. By now, with all the time that’s passed, they could have restored so much of the power supply that I honestly don’t know what to say.
‘Every day, the standard of living falls lower and lower’
Ihor
Sevastopol; about 220 kilometers (137 miles) from mainland Ukraine
I don’t have a car, so the fuel crisis hasn’t hit me the way it has drivers, but it’s still affected me, as supply issues have pushed up prices at supermarkets. At Yeda Voda, for example, shelves were half-empty in early August. There’s also a big problem with Ozon, which has stopped accepting orders from Crimea; [local media] report that its warehouses are overflowing and nothing is being delivered.
Power is cut every day, sometimes for up to eight hours. Usually there’s no electricity from 6 to 8 a.m., then it comes on for four hours before going off again for another four. I work from home, so all of this is genuinely disruptive, and I rely on mobile internet to get by. I haven’t bought a generator since it’s impractical in an apartment, and gas is expensive anyway.
I don’t go to the beach — that’s just how much of a typical local I am. But even on the street, I notice fewer people and cars than last year. Every day, the standard of living falls lower and lower.
Sometimes strikes happen almost every day; other times there’s a lull for about a month. A missile recently hit near my house at 5 a.m., and it was terrifying. At moments like that I hide in the bathroom, though if it hits the house directly, nothing will help, since we have gas. Just as you start getting used to it, another strike comes, and it’s frightening all over again.
I have plenty of reasons not to leave. Just when it seems like it’s time to pack up, something happens [in my personal life] that makes leaving impossible. Plus, I don’t know where I’d go — so for now, I’m staying put.
I just wish Ukraine would come back and life could return to normal. Of course, it will never truly be like before, but at least this whole situation would somehow be resolved.
‘My husband’s workweek was cut from five days to three’
Inga
Ukromnoye, Simferopol district; about 130 kilometers (81 miles) from mainland Ukraine
I live with my husband and our three children. Overall, the power situation is manageable, but on days when it’s out for 5–6 hours, food in the freezer thaws and spoils. Our water comes from a well, so when the power goes, so does the water — we stock up whenever it’s running. We bought a 75,000-ruble generator for the house, essentially a battery that charges up and then supplies electricity.
My husband works in a neighboring village, where the power is often out for entire days, coming and going unpredictably. His company installed a generator too. His workweek was cut from five days to three, and we lost a third of our income. He’s currently our family’s only breadwinner, and I’m afraid he could be out of work entirely by winter if things keep going this way.
Supermarket prices have gone up by 30%. Cheaper chains like “Ambar” have half-empty shelves, though other stores still have a decent selection.
We’ve driven to the mainland three times for gas, buying 200 liters (53 gallons) each trip — it’s cheaper, and the fuel quality is better there.
During shelling we hide with the kids in the bathroom, though it’s been quiet lately. Our oldest, 17, understands everything and is scared just like we are. The middle child, 7, mostly sleeps through it, and so does the youngest, who’s a year old.
We thought about leaving at one point, but for now we’ve decided to stay. With three kids it’s complicated — our oldest is entering his final year of school, and the middle child is just starting. We’ve decided to get through the winter here and see what comes after that.
‘How my animals and I will stay warm this winter is a mystery’
Anna
A village in northwestern Crimea
The district where I was born and still live borders Ukraine by sea. I moved to the district center when I was young, then came back in 2014.
My return coincided with the neighboring state [how Anna refers to Ukraine] declaring a blockade of the peninsula. Many vacation resorts around the village closed as a result, since visitors stopped coming, and the dogs that had guarded those resorts were abandoned. They ran into the village looking for food among the people there.
I felt sorry for them, so I started feeding some and tried to find homes for others through social media, but I wasn’t able to place a single one.
It had the opposite effect: once people saw my posts, they started bringing animals to me from all over the district. Someone once just walked up and tied an adult dog to my fence. Others brought me animals found on the road with broken legs, or rescued from conflict zones. Several small puppies were pulled out literally from under a lawnmower.
In total, I now have 90 cats and 30 dogs. My property has no kennels or other special facilities — they all live with me at home, with some staying with relatives and others at abandoned vacation resorts. I’m a pensioner, and almost nobody helps me. It’s impossible to support that many animals on a single welfare payment, so I rely on people who care to pitch in.
The power problems started sometime in July, though I don’t remember exactly when, since I spend all my time busy with the animals. At first there was no electricity for two days, then it came back briefly before going out again for another two days. Then something serious happened, and we went five days without electricity, water, or gas.
Since I usually feed the animals porridge instead of store-bought pet food, I had to cook for myself and for them over an open fire. Fortunately, the administration brought me and other village residents a free gas canister in early August, but I’m almost afraid to even look at it or breathe on it — I’m trying to conserve it.
We recently bought an electric hot plate and cook on it whenever there’s power. Today [August 10] there was no power at all, so I had to give the animals dry food. The electricity now gets turned on and off at random, with no schedule at all, but we’ve adapted.
I used to buy pet food from Wildberries and Ozon, but now they refuse to deliver here. It’s more expensive at the store, and the nearest one is 25 kilometers (16 miles) away — I don’t have a car, but people help out.
When there are strikes, the animals get anxious. The dogs often start barking even before a drone alert comes in. I head for the bathroom, and the dogs and cats scatter to their hiding spots.
I’ve never even considered leaving the village. My relatives once told me, “If there’s an evacuation, leave them all behind. Health comes first.” But where would I abandon them all? Are they supposed to just die here alone? I’m not going anywhere.
I don’t make big plans — I don’t think beyond tomorrow, and I just deal with things as they come. Winter worries me because we rely on electric heaters. In past winters, only the cats had heating, since they live with me indoors, but heating with convection heaters is expensive, so we saved however we could. Of the eight heaters we needed, only three worked, and five were broken. Building warm enclosures for all the animals is my biggest dream.
How my animals and I will stay warm this winter is a mystery. The other villagers have stoves they can heat with coal and firewood, but no one can imagine how much that will cost.
I try to distance myself from the situation we’re in. I do my own thing, and I’m grateful to the animals for keeping me distracted.
More than anything, I want peace.
‘If the accumulated problems aren’t solved urgently, there will be a revolt’
Oleh
Dzhankoi; about 40 kilometers (25 miles) from mainland Ukraine
I live in Dzhankoi. We had no electricity at all from July 5 to 16. Starting July 17, power was supplied irregularly for 2–4 hours a day, at a catastrophically low voltage of 120–140 volts, or 150 if we were lucky. In some villages, it doesn’t even reach 100 volts.
At that voltage, basic appliances like refrigerators and washing machines would either fail to turn on at all, in the best case, or literally burn out in the worst. I was careful with mine — or maybe just lucky — and nothing burned out. To avoid the risk, I bought a voltage stabilizer, but it doesn’t help much, since most models don’t work at input voltages below 150 volts.
In August, daytime temperatures in Crimea reach nearly 40 degrees Celsius (104 degrees Fahrenheit), so without a refrigerator, food spoils within hours, and I had to forget about air conditioning entirely. A neighbor with a generator saved me by running power to my refrigerator for four hours a day. Stable power was restored in Dzhankoi on August 12, though in the surrounding villages, the situation still leaves much to be desired.
I live on the first floor and have been lucky with water — it’s almost always available. It’s much harder for village residents and for Dzhankoi residents on higher floors, since the water supply depends on electricity. For them it often comes out as a thin trickle for 2–3 hours, and sometimes there’s no water at all for a whole day.
Food prices have risen noticeably. Perishable goods like vegetables, fruit, and sausages have disappeared from stores, though everything else is still available.
Overall, people are desperate — they’ve been pushed to the limit. If the accumulated problems aren’t solved urgently, there will be a revolt.
I’ve thought about moving, but for now, that’s all it is — a thought.
‘I’m getting by however I can, and I’m not planning to leave’
Anton
Alupka; about 980 kilometers (609 miles) from mainland Ukraine
Starting around July 21, the city went four days straight without power. Now it’s supplied from 6 a.m. to 10 p.m. Conditions are worse in other cities, but we may get more [electricity] because we have no gas.
I recently passed through Yalta and saw people crowding outside supermarkets to charge their phones, since the stores had put out extension cords. We’ve had something similar here too, but only during total power outages.
I have a car and a scooter, but I haven’t been to a gas station in a while. I only heard that [Kremlin-appointed Crimea head Sergey] Aksyonov [as of August 4] set the price of 92-octane gasoline at 100 rubles. In early July, I drove to the mainland and brought back 100 liters (26 gallons) of gasoline, waiting in line eight times at four different stations over the course of a day. People around me were tense and angry.
The last time I filled up was in early August, at 190 rubles, with no lines at all. I just drove up and that was it. The most I’ve ever paid was 275 rubles, and resellers have charged as much as 350, even 500 rubles. But what choice do you have?
I ride a motorcycle to work now to save fuel. Since the start of August, I’ve been working as an assistant at a private villa. Before that I worked at a factory, but construction was frozen due to logistics problems along the “Novorossiya” highway.
I used to give tours for tourists every summer, and my pay depended on how much work I did. This year there are no tourists at all, so I didn’t even bother trying.
These days I hardly go anywhere except work — only on weekends do I treat myself to the beach. Everyone there is local; I can tell from the license plates.
In Crimea they banned riding motorcycles from 10 p.m. to 6 a.m., saying they sound like drones — they can tow your scooter to an impound lot and fine you 30,000 rubles. I once got lost near Sudak and had to sleep on a mountain pass; luckily, I had a sleeping bag and a hammock with me, and something was being bombed in the distance all night. Now I always race home by 9:30 to make it in time.
Drones almost never fly over Alupka. There was only one time, [July 22], when I heard explosions at night, after which the power went out. But near Sevastopol, where I vacationed last year, there was constant cannon fire. It was scary.
Because of the power outages, various products disappeared from supermarkets for a while — dairy, for example — but now there are almost no empty shelves anywhere. The one thing I’ve noticed missing is cigarettes. At Yeda Voda, 70% of the products are gone. Only vodka is left. Other stores bought generators and reorganized how they operate.
At the store near my house, while there was no power, employees would unscrew the cap off a bottle of water I wanted to buy, keep it, and screw on a different one. That way, once the power came back, they could scan the item into the Chestny Znak system. Sellers also copied barcodes into a notebook by hand.
Prices have gone up by about 30%. I used to buy the “Adrenaline” energy drink for 110 rubles; now it costs 160. Camping gas canisters have gotten a lot more expensive too — they used to cost 100 rubles, peaked at 250, and now sell for 170. These canisters are the main lifesaver for people when the power goes out.
I’m getting by however I can, and I’m not planning to leave. My mother is here, and I don’t want to abandon her. The mood, of course, isn’t great, but we’re living one day at a time. Back in late May there was still confidence that the tourist season would take off and we’d be able to earn good money. This summer, there’s no hope of that.
Winter is coming soon, and I hope I’ll be able to earn at least a little money to buy alternative energy sources — a big gas canister, say — so I’ll have something to cook and heat the apartment with.
I really want all of this to end.
