articles.title: Russia’s missile tests around disputed islands anger Japan
articles.body:
Japan has criticised missile tests carried out by Russia’s navy around the disputed islands visited by Vladimir Putin last week amid continuing tensions between the two countries.
Russia’s Pacific fleet said on Thursday that it had fired Bastion surface-to-ship missiles from Etorofu, the largest island in the disputed archipelago, simulating an attack on enemy vessels, hitting all of its targets approximately 300km away.
Officials said the drills included a nuclear-powered submarine and a guided-missile cruiser, according to reports.
Putin sparked a tit-for-tat summoning of ambassadors in Tokyo and Moscow with his first visit last week to Etorofu, the largest of the group of four islands. They are referred to as the Northern Territories or Four Northern Islands in Japan, and as part of the Kuril Islands in Russia.
Toshimitsu Motegi, Japan’s foreign minister, said on Thursday during a trip to Oman: “We cannot tolerate moves to strengthen military power on the Four Northern Islands because they go against our country’s stance [on the territories].”
Territorial rows over the islands go back to the 19th century. The Soviet Union seized them from Japan at the end of the second world war.
Exercises by the Russian fleet began on 4 August and Japan was informed in advance that they would include live-fire drills. Japan lodged a protest against the large-scale manoeuvres on 5 August.
According to the Russian news agency Tass, the drills involved “approximately 60 surface ships, submarines, and support vessels, about 30 aircraft, helicopters, and unmanned aerial systems of the Pacific fleet’s naval aviation, as well as over 13,000 service members”.
Putin observed some of the exercises from the Varyag on 12 August as part of his trip to the disputed islands and to Sakhalin, the large undisputedly Russian island north of Hokkaido.
“The region is unfortunately becoming increasingly prone to conflict, with Nato seeking to gain a foothold here and the emergence of new military and political blocs,” said Putin, speaking aboard the flagship. “There are efforts and plans to deploy new weapons systems here, which creates threats for our country.”
The Russian drills are scheduled to continue through 29 August.

articles.title: The Atlantic: Zelenskyy was reportedly offered plan to strike Moscow airports with drones
articles.body:
The Atlantic: Zelenskyy was reportedly offered plan to strike Moscow airports with drones
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was reportedly offered a plan in early 2026 to launch large-scale drone strikes against airports in Moscow and Moscow Oblast.
Source: The Atlantic, citing two people familiar with the situation
Quote: "Early this year, Ukrainian officials came to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy with a risky new plan to end the war with Russia. It would require expanding their bombing campaign to include a set of targets and a class of weapons they had long avoided."
Details: According to two sources cited by The Atlantic, officials proposed expanding Ukrainian strikes to Moscow's airports using drones equipped with artificial intelligence. The aim would have been to disrupt the operations of international airlines flying to and from the Russian capital.
If conducted, the plan would have been unprecedented in the history of warfare. It envisaged swarms of autonomous drones equipped with AI-based navigation systems independently locating and striking targets without being controlled by an operator.
According to the journalists, similar systems have been tested by various countries, including the US, in recent years. Meanwhile, the legality of their use is the subject of an ongoing debate because of the potential for violations of international humanitarian law. No country has yet used such systems in combat.
The Atlantic reported that the plan was presented to Zelenskyy in the winter. The Ukrainian president expressed serious concern about the potential threat to civilian aviation, including the risk of accidentally striking a passenger aircraft or killing civilians near the airports.
Despite these concerns, Zelenskyy, seeking a way to put pressure on Russia and revive the peace process, allowed preparations for such strikes to continue for some time, The Atlantic said.
The Atlantic reported that by mid-spring, preparations had progressed sufficiently far and the project had been given the name M&M's.
The Atlantic said former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov played a key role in the project. According to the sources, he was involved in assembling a team of developers, developing AI-based guidance systems and seeking funding to produce large numbers of autonomous UAVs.
However, preparations for the operation were subsequently halted.
A representative from the Office of the President of Ukraine denied the information in comments to The Atlantic, calling the claims false.
There is currently no official confirmation that such a plan was developed or existed.
Background:
- Moscow and Moscow Oblast have come under repeated drone attacks in recent months. For example, on the night of 18-19 August, Russian authorities again reported a drone attack on Moscow.
- On the night of 17-18 August, the Russian authorities reported that more than 600 drones were heading towards Moscow.
- On the afternoon of 18 August, Russia's Defence Ministry claimed that more than 1,600 drones had been shot down over a 24-hour period, along with 10 guided aerial bombs and two HIMARS rockets.

Days After Putin’s First Visit, Russia Fires Missiles Near Islands Claimed by Japan
Days after Putin’s first-ever visit to the disputed Kuril Islands, Russia staged rare missile drills nearby—using a nuclear submarine, a missile cruiser, and a Bastion coastal system in a fresh show of force toward Japan.
Russia has carried out rare missile drills involving naval vessels and a ground-based launcher near the disputed southern Kuril Islands, adding to already heightened tensions with Japan, Bloomberg reported on August 21.
Russia’s Pacific Fleet said missiles were launched from a nuclear-powered submarine, a missile cruiser, and a Bastion coastal defense system operating in the area of the southern Kurils. The fleet did not specify when the exercises took place.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the Russian military, the missiles were fired at targets located more than 300 kilometers, or about 186 miles, away and successfully struck them.
The Pacific Fleet did not disclose the exact location of the drills. Russia has, however, deployed Bastion coastal defense batteries on Iturup, known in Japan as Etorofu, since 2016.
The exercises drew a sharp reaction from Tokyo.
“Russia’s military buildup on the four Northern Islands runs counter to Japan’s position and is unacceptable,” Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi told reporters.
The southern Kuril Islands have remained under Russian control since Soviet forces seized them from Japan in the final days of World War II. Tokyo continues to claim Iturup, Kunashir, Shikotan, and the Habomai islets, collectively referring to them as the Northern Territories.
The missile drills came only days after Russian leader Vladimir Putin made his first visit to the disputed territory, traveling to Iturup last week. Japan formally protested that visit as well.
The long-running territorial dispute has prevented Russia and Japan from signing a formal peace treaty since World War II.
The latest military activity also comes as Japan continues to support Ukraine against Russia’s war of aggression, including through sanctions on Moscow.
Tokyo has also provided Ukraine with non-lethal military assistance, including body armor and vehicles.
During his recent visit to Russia’s Far East, Putin accused Japan of changing its approach toward Moscow without provocation. He criticized Japanese sanctions and pointed to defense documents in which Tokyo identifies Russia as a serious security threat.
The combination of Putin’s first visit to Iturup and the missile drills has added fresh pressure to one of the longest-running territorial disputes in East Asia, with Moscow now visibly demonstrating strike capabilities near islands Japan still considers its own.
Previously, Russia sent four missile-armed warships near Japan, with the vessels passing about 40 kilometers (25 miles) from Hokkaido a day after Putin visited Iturup, one of the disputed Kuril Islands claimed by Japan.

articles.title: Turkey says it will not fall into Israeli 'trap' in Syria
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Turkey says it will not fall into Israeli 'trap' in Syria, denies military presence in air base
Turkey “will not fall into the trap” set by Israel, the country’s presidency said in a statement, days after Tel Aviv struck the Abu al-Duhur air base located near Aleppo.
"We are experienced enough not to fall into the trap of figures like (Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin) Netanyahu, who aim to undermine peace and stability in our region," said Burhanettin Duran, the Turkish presidency's director of communications.
After the site was struck, causing damage to its runways, reports said that a Turkish delegation had been at the site just hours earlier, but Turkey has denied a military visit to the location.
Israeli media said a Turkish military delegation had been at the site, and a Syrian monitor said the delegation was there as part of efforts to rehabilitate the base.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office said Turkish forces had recently toured the base, warning that Israel would not tolerate a "threat" from a Turkish presence there.
"We will not tolerate a Turkish military entrenchment moving southward, because it threatens us," Netanyahu told an army radio podcast.
The premier's office also said on Tuesday evening that Israel had repeatedly warned Syria that deploying Turkish forces at an airbase near Aleppo would pose a threat to its national security, noting that Damascus had ignored the warnings.
The office stated that Israel and Syria had agreed to maintain the status quo on security matters, claiming that Damascus was on the verge of violating this understanding by allowing the Turkish military deployment.
But Turkish defence ministry spokesman Rear Admiral Zeki Akturk said the strikes were "unacceptable" and that Ankara would act "resolutely" to protect Syria's efforts to establish post-war stability.
"Israel's attack on the Abu al-Zuhur air base is aimed at harming Syria's stability, security, unity, integrity and infrastructure. Attacks violating Syria's sovereignty and territorial integrity are unacceptable," he told journalists.
"In this context, our efforts and contributions to protect Syria's sovereignty and territorial integrity, and help it establish a stable and secure environment, will continue resolutely."
Turkey’s presidency has also clarified that it is not considering retaliation.
Duran said that Netanyahu was "clinging to this irrational stance due to upcoming elections, internal political tensions, and fears. He views hostility toward Turkey as a political lifeline".
The development comes as Syria’s new transitional government has condemned the Israeli strikes, which marked the first time the location was targeted since the fall of the Assad regime.
The US has also rebuked the strikes, with US special envoy to Syria Tom Barrack describing the attack as an "unnecessary escalation" that did not serve regional stability.
Barrack pointed to the approach taken by the government of Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa, saying Damascus "has not adopted a hostile posture nor maintained proxy forces, but has repeatedly demonstrated a preference for de-escalation with Israel".
He also emphasised Washington's efforts to reduce tensions between the two countries.
Barrack called on all sides to prioritise "reasoned dialogue" over further military incidents.
Since the fall of the Assad regime, Israel has stepped up its raids and incursions into Syria, while targeting much of the country's remaining military infrastructure.
Israeli attacks have struck Syrian air-defence systems, long- and medium-range missiles, weapons and missile depots, scientific research centres and other military facilities.
Israeli strikes have also hit several key Syrian airfields and military installations, including Hama airport, as well as Tiyas, Shayrat, Palmyra, Dumayr and Mezzeh airfields.
Agencies contributed to this report.

articles.title: FSB arrests foreign national over Ukrainian drone plot (VIDEO)
articles.body:
FSB arrests foreign national over Ukrainian drone plot (VIDEO)
Russian security officers have detained a foreign national suspected of surveilling critical infrastructure sites on behalf of Ukrainian intelligence, the Federal Security Service (FSB) announced on Friday.
The suspect was taken into custody this month in Murmansk Region near the border, as he sought to illegally cross into Norway, the agency said in a statement. The detained man is believed to have a longstanding relationship with Kiev’s special services, having voluntarily contacted them back in 2023 for the first time, according to FSB.
The man’s Ukrainian handlers had ordered him to travel to Moscow and conduct reconnaissance at a key train hub “to identify freight trains transporting petroleum products, as well as administrative buildings in the city center,” the FSB said. He was involved in an “attempt to launch an FPV drone” to gather the intelligence, it added.
The Kiev regime has intensified attempts to stage terrorist attacks in Russia to compensate for the mounting pressure it has been experiencing on the frontline, as well as its inability to inflict “meaningful damage on critical infrastructure sites in Moscow Region,” the agency warned. The planned attacks involve short-range kamikaze drones that were supposed to be launched from an immediate vicinity of targeted sites by planted agents and local collaborators recruited online, including victims of fraudulent Ukrainian call centers, the FSB said. Involvement in such activities incurs heavy penalties under Russian law, up to life behind bars, the agency stressed.
Last month, the FSB said it had thwarted a major Ukrainian FPV drone plot, which involved smuggling 24 AI-guided drones into the country and using them to target a key defense industry enterprise and military airfields. The failed operation had been prepared by Kiev’s intelligence with the direct involvement of Western handlers, the agency said at the time.
The disassembled drones had been flown into Russia using fixed-wing UAVs and balloons, which were collected by the suspects and transferred deeper into the country for assembly and preparations for the attack. However, the whole operation had been closely monitored by Russian secret services from the very beginning, and the perpetrators and their accomplices ended up in custody.

articles.title: US aircraft carrier arrives in Middle East, relieving long-deployed USS Lincoln
articles.body:
US aircraft carrier arrives in Middle East, relieving long-deployed USS Lincoln
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Asia-based USS George Washington aircraft carrier is now operating in the Middle East, the U.S. military said Thursday, relieving a long-deployed carrier following reports of mental health challenges and supply shortages aboard while it was supporting the Iran war.
U.S. Central Command, which oversees military operations in the Middle East, said on social media that the carrier arrived in the region Wednesday. It was not clear when the USS Abraham Lincoln would arrive back in the U.S. or whether it would make a port stop along the way, but the journey takes just over a month.
The Washington arrived as concerns have grown about the Lincoln’s lengthy deployment, which has included a record-setting uninterrupted time at sea of more than 250 days, and about reports of crew stress and poor mental health, as well as supply shortages, including food and hygiene products.
Several Democratic lawmakers have pressed the Department of Defense for accountability over conditions aboard the Lincoln, which Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has said were “completely misrepresented.”
Hegseth spoke with the Lincoln’s crew last week, and Adm. Brad Cooper, head of U.S. Central Command, visited this past weekend. In an editorial published Sunday by The Wall Street Journal, Cooper said the crew “delivered a performance for the ages, and now you are going home.”
Extended deployments of carriers wear on service members who are away from home for long periods and increase strain on the ship and its equipment. While renewed hostilities between the U.S. and Iran calmed in recent weeks, the Navy is enforcing a reimposed blockade on Iranian ports in the Strait of Hormuz, and the Trump administration has offered no clarity on how it intends to wind down the war.
Hegseth has said the U.S. can maintain the blockade “indefinitely.”
President Donald Trump this week downplayed reports about conditions on the Lincoln, which left its homeport in San Diego in November and arrived in the Middle East in January. Trump called the nearly nine months at sea that the sailors endured a “good period of time” but added that “over the years, we’ve had them out there much longer.”
Trump told reporters Monday that he spoke with a retired admiral over the weekend who recounted being on ships for “much longer.” Trump said the admiral assured him that the Lincoln is “beautifully maintained and beautifully taken care of.” Trump did not name the admiral.
In a statement Sunday after visiting the Lincoln, Cooper praised the carrier’s leaders for prioritizing mental health and resilience.
“History will record this deployment as one of the most operationally intense and consequential of the modern era,” Cooper said.
The Washington joins the USS George H.W. Bush in the Middle East, leaving Asia without an American carrier strike group at a time when China has shown more signs of aggression.
The lack of a U.S. carrier in the Pacific may be short-lived if the Navy deploys another in the next couple of months. But it shows how the open-ended operations with Iran are running some American sailors ragged, analysts say, while the Trump administration further retreats from the Asia-Pacific region and focuses on the Western Hemisphere.

articles.title: NATO Military Committee to Return to Ukraine After Eight Years
articles.body:
Ukraine expects the NATO Military Committee to visit the country in October, marking its first such visit in eight years, Ukrainian Armed Forces (AFU) Commander-in-Chief Mykhailo Drapatyi said on Friday, Aug. 21.
Drapatyi made the announcement after his first meeting with NATO Military Committee Chair Adm. Giuseppe Cavo Dragone, whom he thanked for his support for Ukraine at the Alliance’s highest military level.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“We are expecting the NATO Military Committee to visit Ukraine in October. The last such visit took place eight years ago,” Drapatyi said in a Facebook post.
Drapatyi said Dragone had visited Ukraine three times and had seen the situation on the ground firsthand.
The Ukrainian commander briefed Dragone on the situation at the front and discussed Ukraine’s military priorities, including long-range strikes, flexible infantry tactics and the use of robotics on the battlefield.
Air defense remains Ukraine’s priority
Drapatyi said air defense was also a key focus of the discussion, describing the protection of Ukrainian airspace as his priority.
“Protecting the sky is my priority,” he said.
He also emphasized that Ukraine is not only receiving military support from NATO allies but is sharing battlefield experience gained during Russia’s full-scale war.
“We are not only receiving support. We are passing on combat experience that no one else has today, and it works for the security of the entire Alliance,” Drapatyi said.

articles.title: British spy plane deploys to Norway for Arctic Stone
articles.body:
An RAF Rivet Joint has deployed to Ørland in Norway for a week-long exercise with the Royal Norwegian Air Force, including training intended to improve interoperability with Norwegian F-35A fighters.
An RAF Rivet Joint intelligence-gathering aircraft has deployed to Ørland in Norway for Exercise Arctic Stone, where British personnel are training alongside the Royal Norwegian Air Force and working with Norwegian F-35A fighters, the UK Defence Journal understands.
According to an RAF news update, the activity is intended to strengthen interoperability between Rivet Joint and Norway’s F-35A fleet while contributing to NATO’s situational awareness on its northern flank.
Operated by 51 Squadron, the RAF’s Rivet Joint specialises in gathering intelligence from signals across the electromagnetic spectrum. Sensors aboard the aircraft allow its crew to intercept and analyse signals while airborne, providing strategic and tactical intelligence that can contribute to a wider picture of military activity and the surrounding security environment. Ground-based specialists from No. 54 Signals Unit also process and exploit the information gathered by the aircraft.
The RAF described the aircraft’s role by stating: “The aircraft specialises in monitoring signals across the electromagnetic spectrum, giving it the ability to deliver real-time strategic and tactical intelligence in a way few other assets can match.” It added that the combination of airborne crews and ground specialists provides commanders with improved situational awareness “day and night, whatever the operational conditions.”
Exercise Arctic Stone is using that capability in two connected roles. RAF personnel are training directly with their Norwegian counterparts, including activities designed to improve cooperation between the Rivet Joint and Norway’s F-35A force, while the intelligence gathered during the deployment is intended to give commanders a clearer assessment of the operating environment.
The RAF said the exercise would allow both air forces to improve their ability to work together within NATO operations.
Norway’s location makes it particularly relevant to NATO operations in the High North, where the Alliance maintains air, maritime and surveillance activity across an area extending towards the Norwegian and Barents Seas. The RAF said the deployment reflected what it described as the region’s “growing strategic importance” and its increasing relevance to NATO’s northern defences and wider European security.
The service said: “As the security picture in the region continues to evolve, the presence of RAF assets working alongside key allies and partners in the area is becoming an ever more important part of how NATO maintains stability on its northern flank.”
Rivet Joint’s role differs from that of conventional airborne surveillance aircraft because its principal focus is the detection and analysis of electromagnetic emissions rather than visual reconnaissance alone. The RAF argues that modern intelligence operations increasingly require information from multiple sources to be combined, particularly as military communications, sensors and other systems become more digitally connected.
The deployment also provides an opportunity to test how intelligence collected by the aircraft can support other platforms operating in the same battlespace. Integration with Norwegian F-35As is intended to improve the exchange and use of information between different aircraft types, while giving personnel experience of operating within a multinational NATO environment.

articles.title: Russia occupied Anton’s home when he was 10. At 18, he volunteered to fight against Ukraine
articles.body:
Now held in a POW camp in western Ukraine, Anton does not consider himself a traitor. He calls Putin “my President” and said he joined Russia’s army to defend “my land,” the BBC reported.
The BBC interviews show what more than a decade of Russian rule has produced in occupied Donbas. Moscow has replaced Ukrainian schools, media, and public institutions while presenting the occupied regions as permanent parts of Russia. It also recruits residents or forces them to fight against Ukraine.
The BBC said prisoners could refuse and were interviewed without guards or cameras.
Almost all its Ukrainian-born interviewees from territories occupied since 2014 said they had enlisted willingly. Anton said he was not a traitor and called Vladimir Putin “my President.”
His friends also volunteered. Messages announcing their deaths followed: “Dead, dead, dead.”
Forced conscription of Ukrainians in occupied territory
One prisoner from Donetsk Oblast told the BBC he had been forced to fight. He wanted only to return to his wife and children.
The BBC cited an official intelligence-based estimate that Russia forcibly conscripted more than 50,000 Ukrainians in occupied areas. It noted that other estimates were higher.
Ukrainian veteran Pavlo Pshenychnyi told Hromadske that occupation authorities used planted drug evidence to push him into Russia’s army. They threatened him with up to 12 years in prison.
Article 51 of the Fourth Geneva Convention prohibits occupying powers from compelling protected residents to serve in their armed forces.
Anton and the Russification of occupied Ukrainian territory
Russia took control of Anton’s home while he was still in primary school. By adulthood, he called himself Russian and dismissed his Ukrainian surname as irrelevant.
Putin’s 2025 policy decree set a 95% target for “all-Russian civic identity” by 2036 and ordered the integration of occupied Ukrainian regions into Russian education, culture, and media.
Kherson-based outlet MOST reported that Russia will introduce compulsory textbooks on 1 September, presenting four occupied Ukrainian regions as historically Russian.
Ukraine’s Center for Countering Disinformation reported in 2025 that more than 100 teenagers from occupied Luhansk attended a Russian military camp. They received firearms, drill, and guard-duty training.
The center described the camp as part of a wider effort to spread Russian war propaganda and hostility toward Ukraine.
Petro Yatsenko of Ukraine’s POW Coordination Headquarters told the BBC that these prisoners were strongly pro-Russian. He said their national identity was “very blurred.”
Ukraine still considers them Ukrainian and treats Russia’s control of their home regions as temporary, the BBC noted.

articles.title: Norway Expands Finnmark Brigade With Artillery and Air Defense
articles.body:
Norway has established three new units within the Finnmark Brigade: an artillery battalion, a combat air defense battery and a communications company.
The Norwegian Armed Forces reported this.
The Norwegian Army says the accelerated formation of the brigade is linked, among other factors, to the deteriorating security situation in Europe. The new structure is intended to strengthen Norway’s military presence in Finnmark, the country’s northernmost region.
The Finnmark Brigade’s artillery battalion is being equipped with K9 VIDAR self-propelled howitzers, Norway’s version of the South Korean K9 Thunder.
The first four K9 VIDAR systems, along with support vehicles, have already arrived at the Garrison of Porsanger.
In 2025, the Norwegian government separately proposed allocating NOK 17 billion to develop the Army. Of that amount, NOK 5.6 billion was earmarked for the procurement of 24 K9 self-propelled howitzers to fully equip the Finnmark Brigade’s artillery battalion.
The K9 VIDAR can engage targets at ranges of more than 40 kilometers. In the future, the system is planned to use ramjet-powered ammunition, which could increase its effective range to more than 120 kilometers.
The formation of the artillery battalion is currently progressing faster than initially planned. The Norwegian Army expects the main conditions for its deployment to be in place by 2028.
The Finnmark Brigade is scheduled to be fully operational by 2033. It will then have around 4,000 personnel, including career soldiers, conscripts and reservists.
When the brigade was established in 2025, it had 280 permanent personnel. Their number is expected to increase to around 350 in fall 2026 and to 700-800 by 2033.
Finnmark Brigade commander Brig. Gen. Jon Olav Fuglem said the creation of the new units has already strengthened the military presence in the region. At the same time, the brigade needs new barracks, housing, offices and other infrastructure for further expansion.
Late last year, Norway announced plans to significantly strengthen its 198-kilometer border with Russia. The plans included new fencing, modern surveillance systems and drones for aerial monitoring.

articles.title: UK-German strike programme includes hypersonic weapon
articles.body:
The UK and Germany are jointly developing deep-strike options including a stealthy cruise missile and a hypersonic glide vehicle, with both countries working towards outline entry into service during the 2030s.
The UK and Germany are working on both stealthy cruise missile and hypersonic glide vehicle solutions under their joint Deep Precision Strike programme, with outline in-service dates extending into the 2030s, the UK Defence Journal understands.
Defence Minister Luke Pollard provided further detail on the programme in a written parliamentary answer to Conservative MP Stuart Anderson, who asked what the UK’s partnership with Germany on deep precision strike weapons entails.
Pollard confirmed that a Memorandum of Understanding signed by the two countries in March 2026 has allowed British and German teams to begin aligning their military requirements and jointly examining technical solutions with industry.
He said: “The UK and Germany signed a Memorandum of Understanding in March 2026 which has enabled joint activities, including with industry, to align military requirements and invest in technical solutions under the Deep Precision Strike programme.”
The programme is examining two distinct missile approaches. Pollard confirmed: “The programme includes Stealthy Cruise and Hypersonic Glide Vehicle missile solutions.”
A stealthy cruise missile would broadly pursue survivability through reduced detectability and a powered flight profile, while a hypersonic glide vehicle represents a different technical approach, travelling at hypersonic speed following launch and manoeuvring towards its target. The parliamentary answer does not provide performance figures, ranges or details of the propulsion and launch arrangements envisaged for either solution, of course.
Pollard said the two governments had reached what he described as “positive alignment” on some of the principal requirements for the programme. He said: “There is positive alignment between the UK and Germany on key programme parameters, including operational concepts and outline target in service dates into the 2030s.”
The wording indicates that the programme remains at a relatively early technical and requirements stage, with the two countries working towards common operational concepts before later development and procurement decisions. British and German teams are currently overseeing technical work already placed with industry while preparing the next stage of contracting.
Pollard said: “Joint UK and Germany teams are now focused on delivering the currently contracted technical work with industry as well as shaping follow on contracts, underpinned in the UK by the funding outlined under the Defence Investment Plan.”
The Deep Precision Strike effort forms part of growing UK-German defence cooperation and is intended to address future requirements for weapons capable of striking targets at considerable distance. The latest answer is significant in explicitly identifying both stealthy cruise and hypersonic glide vehicle solutions as components of the work, while also placing the anticipated service timeframe in the 2030s.
The current phase is focused on technical work with industry, alignment of military requirements and the preparation of follow-on contracts as Britain and Germany determine how the programme will progress towards development and eventual fielding.

articles.title: Ukraine says 2 killed, 8 injured in Russian overnight strikes on Kharkiv, Sumy regions
articles.body:
Kanyshai Butun
21 August 2026•Update: 21 August 2026
Two people were killed and eight others injured in overnight Russian strikes on Ukraine’s Kharkiv and Sumy regions, local authorities said.
Kharkiv Gov. Oleh Syniehubov said two people were killed and two others injured in Russian strikes that damaged civilian infrastructure.
In Sumy region, six people were injured, including a 16-year-old girl, Gov. Oleh Hryhorov said.
In the Odesa region, a Russian drone attack damaged the Tabaky border checkpoint with Moldova, prompting authorities to suspend operations, Ukraine’s State Border Guard Service said.
“The Moldovan side has been informed about the situation,” it said.
Separately, Ukraine’s General Staff claimed Russia launched 135 drones overnight, 107 of which were suppressed in northern, southern and eastern parts of the country.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukrainian strikes hit an oil refinery in Russia’s Perm region, more than 1,600 kilometers (1,000 miles) from the border, and the Marinovka military air base in the Volgograd region. He added that there were also “results in the Black Sea.”
Zelenskyy said a Russian Su-34 fighter jet was damaged in a previous strike on the Akhtubinsk air base, while a facility used to store, prepare and launch attack drones was hit in Primorsko-Akhtarsk.
Perm Gov. Dmitry Makhonin confirmed a Ukrainian drone attack on the region, saying one person was injured and an industrial facility was damaged. He did not identify the facility.
Russia’s Defense Ministry claimed its forces intercepted or destroyed 325 Ukrainian drones overnight across the federation, annexed Crimea and waters of Azov and Black Seas.
It also claimed that Moscow struck Ukrainian port infrastructure used by the troops, including warehouses containing weapons, military equipment and supplies at the port of Reni.
Independent verification of the claims remains difficult due to the ongoing war.

articles.title: Royal Navy ends four-month command of NATO task group
articles.body:
Commodore Maryla Ingham has handed command of Standing NATO Maritime Group One to French Rear Admiral Nicolas Molitor after four months spanning Baltic Sentry, Arctic operations, major anti-submarine exercises and a deployment across the Atlantic.
The Royal Navy has completed four months in command of Standing NATO Maritime Group One, handing leadership of the alliance task group to France after operations stretching from the Baltic and High North to the eastern seaboard of the United States, the UK Defence Journal understands.
Commodore Maryla Ingham formally handed command to French Rear Admiral Nicolas Molitor in Reykjavik, Iceland, bringing to an end a tenure that began in April and included Baltic Sentry, Arctic Sentry, Exercise Dynamic Mongoose and the US-led FLEETEX 250. According to a Royal Navy news update, the task group also supported protection of critical national infrastructure, anti-submarine warfare, boarding operations, gunnery, casualty evacuation and multinational integration across several maritime theatres.
The handover follows an interview with UK Defence Journal last month in which Ingham described the pace and breadth of the deployment while speaking from her flagship at sea in the middle of a gunnery shoot. She said the group had moved almost immediately into Baltic Sentry after taking command, spending around a month on the operation before heading north for Dynamic Mongoose 26 off Norway, a major anti-submarine exercise involving three live submarines, five maritime patrol aircraft and a multinational surface force.
Ingham told UK Defence Journal: “We started off in April. We went straight into enhanced vigilance activity, Baltic Sentry, which is to protect critical underwater infrastructure, and we were there for about a month.” She continued: “Then we went up off Norway, and we were the lead for Exercise Dynamic Mongoose 26, which was a major ASW exercise, multinational, three live submarines, five MPAs. Goodness, I can’t even remember how many ships we had.”
From there, the group crossed the Atlantic for FLEETEX 250, a US Second Fleet-led exercise which at one point expanded to ten ships, before taking part in the International Naval Review marking the 250th anniversary of the United States Navy in New York. The Royal Navy said the wider exercise involved 30 warships operating off Virginia and North Carolina. Ingham subsequently described the group’s integration into the Commander Task Force Atlantic activation as particularly important because it demonstrated multinational command and control across the surface, air and underwater domains.
She told UK Defence Journal that the activity was “all about demonstrating command and control of multinational forces on the sea, in the air, and underwater, and that’s the first time that’s been practised.” After returning across the Atlantic, the group called at Glasgow before heading back to sea for gunnery and operations in the High North ahead of the eventual handover in Iceland.
One of the most tangible operational changes during Ingham’s command came through Baltic Sentry, where NATO has increased its focus on protecting subsea cables, pipelines and other critical infrastructure. Ingham said the operation had reduced NATO’s reaction time to incidents involving critical underwater infrastructure from around 17 hours to approximately one hour. She also described a Baltic operating picture in which almost all activity could now be observed or tracked by the alliance.
“It’s also reduced our reaction time to critical underwater incidents from around 17 hours to an hour,” she said. “And it’s really enhanced our situational awareness.” She added: “I’m really confident that there is very little that happens in the Baltic without us being aware of it.”
The group encountered Russian naval forces during the deployment, although Ingham characterised those interactions as routine and professional rather than confrontational. “Did we have interactions with the Russian Navy? Yes, we did. But they were all safe and professional,” she said. “At the end of the day, a lot of those areas are international waters, and we all patrol them together, because that’s the nature of the sea.”
She repeatedly spoke on the protection of seabed infrastructure as one of the group’s central missions, arguing that the Baltic operation had improved not just the quantity of forces available but the way they were coordinated. British, French, Spanish and Turkish ships were among those contributing to Baltic Sentry, alongside aircraft and other NATO capabilities. Ingham said the alliance now had considerably more maritime assets available for such tasks than Russia and was using them in a more structured way.
Another distinctive feature of the deployment was the way the British command staff operated from allied warships. Ingham and her Royal Navy battle staff initially commanded from the German frigate FGS Sachsen before transferring to the Canadian frigate HMCS Ville de Québec, the first time a Royal Navy-led task group had commanded operations successively from ships belonging to two different allied navies. The Royal Navy said this reflected the level of trust and integration within the group.
Ingham made the same point more practically during her interview with UK Defence Journal, describing NATO naval interoperability as something embedded in everyday procedures rather than simply an aspiration. “Out of the 32 nations in NATO, over 25 of them are maritime nations, and we all operate using the same tactics, techniques and procedures,” she said. “So it’s actually really, really seamless to be able to operate in another ship, and we’ve proven that.”
She used replenishment at sea as one example. NATO ships use common fittings and procedures, allowing vessels from different nations to refuel from one another without lengthy adaptation. “Any NATO ship can fuel off any NATO tanker,” Ingham said. “Everybody knows what to expect. Everybody knows how to do it. Everybody practises it. And so when you need to fuel, you’re literally in, fuel, gone.”
The Royal Navy also contributed a Wildcat helicopter from 815 Naval Air Squadron while the staff was embarked in FGS Sachsen, adding surveillance, reconnaissance and force-protection capability. Ships from France, Germany, Belgium, Denmark, the Netherlands, Portugal, Turkey, Spain, Norway, Canada and the United States served with the group at different points during the deployment.
Ingham said, as quoted in the Royal Navy update: “Leading Standing NATO Maritime Group One has been a great privilege. I am incredibly proud of my Battle Staff and the ships from across the Alliance that have served alongside us, demonstrating NATO’s unwavering commitment to collective defence and deterrence.”
She added: “Throughout my tenure, we have shown that our strength at sea comes not from any one Nation, but from the unity, trust and professionalism that bind us together as Allies. In an increasingly complex security environment, that solidarity remains our greatest strategic advantage.”
That reflected the argument she made to UK Defence Journal when asked what the standing maritime group ultimately exists to achieve. “The first one is deterrence, and we mustn’t ever forget that this is a deterrent alliance,” she said, before pointing to Britain’s dependence on maritime trade and undersea communications. She cited 95% of UK imports arriving by sea, around half of its food and 97% of internet data travelling through subsea cables.
For Ingham, the deployment also demonstrated the less visible value of a standing multinational force. “We’re specialist mariners. We are professional, calm, getting on with our jobs. We are not looking for trouble,” she said. “We’re a defensive alliance here to defend over a billion people.”
The handover in Reykjavik brings Ingham’s fifth command at sea to an end and her first commanding a multinational battle staff. Her own description of command remained notably simple despite the scale of the task group: “Execute the mission. Two, keep the ship safe. Three, look after your people.”
Rear Admiral Nicolas Molitor now assumes responsibility for SNMG1 as the standing force continues NATO’s maritime deterrence and defence mission across northern European and Atlantic waters.

articles.title: Russia attacks Ukraine-Moldova border checkpoint for second night in a row
articles.body:
Russia attacks Ukraine-Moldova border checkpoint for second night in a row
Russia struck Ukraine’s Odesa region with drones overnight on August 21, hitting the Tabaky international checkpoint on the border with Moldova, Ukraine’s State Border Guard Service reported.
The attack damaged the checkpoint’s buildings and structures, forcing it to close. Traffic is now being redirected to other border crossings.
It’s the second attack on a border checkpoint in the past 24 hours. The day before, amid a massive strike on Kyiv, Russian forces also struck a border checkpoint on the border with Moldova in the Odesa region, among other targets, Volodymyr Zelensky said. Foreign Ministry head Andrii Sybiha added that these are “not isolated incidents,” saying Russia “is increasingly testing the resolve of NATO and its partners by violating the sovereignty of neighboring countries.”
Moldova’s Defense Ministry reported that a drone entered the country’s airspace overnight on August 20, amid the strikes on Ukraine. Preliminary data indicate it was a Shahed-136, the Russian modification known as Geran-2.

articles.title: Over 11,000 Zanoza FPV drones delivered to special military op zone — manufacturer
articles.body:
MOSCOW, August 21. TASS/. More than 11,000 Zanoza FPV drones of various models have been delivered to Russia’s special military operation zone in Ukraine since 2022, the manufacturer, Zanoza Drones, told TASS.
"The 10-inch Zanoza-10 FPV drone, developed by Urals specialists, is being successfully deployed across all key sectors of the battle contact line, where it has proven its effectiveness despite the enemy’s intense electronic warfare. To date, total deliveries exceed 11,000 drones in various configurations: of these, more than 10,000 are standard radio-controlled versions and over 1,000 are specialized fiber-optic-controlled drones. "We are not resting on our laurels: active work is underway to increase the range of the fiber-optic versions, while paying special attention to maintaining the reliability of the communication channel and reducing the risk of signal loss at maximum ranges," the company stated.
The company specified that it continues to improve the drones based on combat experience and feedback from Russian military personnel. "Based on feedback from the front, we carried out a comprehensive upgrade of the Zanoza-10 hardware component, significantly enhancing protection against external and onboard interference, which guarantees the stability and clarity of the radio signal under the harshest combat conditions," the manufacturer noted.
The Zanoza series drones are designed to carry a warhead of up to 3.5 kg over a distance of up to 40 km. "The drone’s confirmed strike range under real-world conditions reaches 42 km. The drone is effective not only as a means of engaging armored targets, vehicles, and fortifications. It can be used for reconnaissance, as well as for delivering necessary supplies to the combat zone. The fiber-optic version of the drone is completely immune to electronic jamming and is equipped with 15-, 20-, and 25-km cables," the company emphasized.

articles.title: Britain to test powerful new anti-ship missile in 2028
articles.body:
The Ministry of Defence says the Stratus future cruise and anti-ship missile programme is approaching its Demonstration Phase, with full-scale system testing scheduled to begin in 2028 and integration planned for Typhoon, Rafale and Royal Navy Type 26 frigates.
The first full-scale system tests of the UK’s Stratus future cruise and anti-ship missile are scheduled to begin in 2028, with development work already completed on the airframe, engine, warhead and seeker, the UK Defence Journal understands.
New parliamentary answers from Defence Minister Luke Pollard provide an update on the programme formerly known as the Future Cruise/Anti-Ship Weapon, or FC/ASW, which is being developed with European partners. Responding to Conservative MP James Cartlidge, Pollard said Stratus was continuing to raise its technology readiness and system maturity through modelling, subsystem testing and trials.
Pollard said: “To date, the programme has completed testing of the airframe design, engine demonstration, warhead and seeker performance. The first full scale system tests are scheduled from 2028.”
A separate answer to Conservative MP Ben Obese-Jecty confirmed that the programme remains on schedule and is expected to move into its Demonstration Phase shortly. Pollard said: “The Stratus programme with our European partners continues to progress to schedule. Development of the weapons and sub-systems is maturing, and the programme will transition soon to its Demonstration Phase.”
The Ministry of Defence also confirmed that Stratus weapons are planned for integration across both air and maritime platforms. Pollard said the weapon systems would be integrated “variously to Typhoon, Rafale and selected naval platforms including the Royal Navy’s Type 26 frigate.”
Stratus is intended to provide the UK and its partners with a new generation of long-range strike and anti-ship weapons. In British service, the programme is intended to succeed capabilities currently provided by Storm Shadow for deep strike and Harpoon for anti-ship warfare, although the precise configuration and performance of the future weapons remain sensitive.
The MOD has now given a further indication of the intended performance of the low-observable version of Stratus. Asked directly for its range, Pollard declined to provide a figure on security grounds but said it would considerably exceed the weapons it is replacing.
He said: “As he will recall from his time as a Defence Minister, the operational range for the Stratus LO missile is classified information. However, the range is significantly greater than the Storm Shadow and Harpoon weapons that it is replacing.”
That statement does not provide a specific range, however, but it confirms that the MOD expects the low-observable Stratus weapon to offer substantially greater reach than either of the existing British systems cited in the answer.
Storm Shadow is an air-launched cruise missile used for long-range strikes against fixed or hardened targets, while Harpoon is a ship-launched anti-ship missile used against surface vessels.
The planned Type 26 integration is particularly relevant to the Royal Navy, which is introducing eight of the anti-submarine warfare frigates.

articles.title: Behind the lens with the Royal Navy’s photographers
articles.body:
The images that carry the Royal Navy onto front pages, and into the pages of this publication, are taken by a small branch of serving sailors who deploy alongside the ships and units they photograph, and a new film released for World Photography Day gives an account of the work in their own words.
Made by the photographers themselves, it runs from a Type 45 destroyer firing Sea Viper in anger for the first time to Royal Marines under fire in Helmand, to military funerals at home.
Helena Burkett, a serving photographer, said: “As photographers, we have an incredible reach for the limited personnel that we actually have in the branch. We capture everything important that’s going on in the navy or the marines, and we push it out globally. Everything you see has something to do with the navy, and it is most likely done by one of our RN photographers.”
That output is what makes coverage of the Royal Navy possible at all. Almost every photograph of a British warship, submarine or Royal Marine that appears in the press, on this website included, was taken by one of these sailors and released through Defence Imagery under the Open Government Licence. Without them there would be a great deal of writing about the fleet and very little showing of it.
One contributor put the point plainly: “You can write and tell people what Lydia does, but you’re never going to reach as many people than you will with a photographer.” Another said: “Without our photos and without our video to show what events really look like, you can’t tell that story successfully. You can’t tell that story in words.”
The Red Sea
Petty Officer Sellers, a photographer based in Portsmouth, was flown out to join HMS Diamond in the Red Sea and slept with his camera bag beside him. He said: “As soon as that general alarm goes, I need to get to the bridge in seconds. I’d have my bag next to me at all times, ready to go, and I would be there because I know I need to capture that image if that missile fires.”
The photograph he took shows a young officer of the watch shielding his face, one eye on the bridge and one protected from the flash to preserve his night vision. He said: “Got that edited, sent back, and within a few hours, turned Sky News on. Breaking news background was that image. Pretty unbelievable to know that was my work, but I think also for the ship to see that image was a great boost of morale, to show the world that everyone knew what they were doing.”
He added: “You’ve got a lot of pressure on your shoulders to make sure you capture the right thing at the right time. If you miss that opportunity, that’s gone. But if you capture it, you’ve got that there for life.” He also noted that the role does not exempt him from the rest of the job. “They need people to look out. I’ve still got that ability to do that whilst I’m up there.”
Afghanistan
The film also features Sean Clee, a former Royal Navy photographer who deployed with the Royal Marines on Operation Herrick 5. He said: “We found ourselves being deployed on every major operation. It was our job to report what was going on, to let the world know what was going on. We were travelling all the time. Just our kit on our back, in and out of Bastion.”
He described being caught in a Taliban ambush while photographing a mortar crew. “As I was taking pictures of the mortar, dropping it in, lads dropping down, an RPG come over, went straight through the roof. The shrapnel just come back on us. Blew me outside of the mortar pit. Turn around, the lad who bent over from the mortar got up, I got a piece of metal sticking out of his head.”
He said: “If I could describe it as anything, it was like the opening scene from Saving Private Ryan, where your ears are ringing and you don’t know what’s going on. It was just like that, just smoke everywhere, dust everywhere.”
Funerals
Helena Burkett, a serving Royal Navy photographer, said the work swings between extremes. She said: “Being a photographer, your job changes a lot. You could be flying out of a helicopter one day, you could be doing a funeral the next day.”
Another photographer in the film described that side of the work at length: “I can find doing funerals difficult. Purely just seeing the family’s grief, it is hard, but it’s at the family’s discretion whether they want a photographer or not. Some people want to remember the day. Some people have passed away that have small children that couldn’t attend the funeral because they’re just too young.”
She described crying on the bus between a church and a burial site before composing herself for the next part of the job, and said: “I do my best to prepare for it emotionally, but I just think this isn’t about me. The families are going through a really horrible time, and I just want to do my best for them at the end of the day.”
She said the branch also demands independence. “There’s no one else that’s going to hold your hand for you or do the job for you. It can be lonely. There’s no one else on board a ship that understands your role to the extent that you do.”
Her standout assignment was on Carrier Strike Group last year aboard HMS Prince of Wales, shooting portraits of shipmates in Tokyo. She was also sent to HMS Dragon with 48 hours notice and was away for three months.
Why it matters now
Several contributors tie the branch’s value to the volume of synthetic imagery now circulating online.
One said: “We know that the world is flooded with imagery, but a lot of it’s not real. A lot of it’s AI. We know that people that aren’t generally friendly to the UK are flooding this country with information that’s probably not real. We don’t lie about what we do. The important thing is that you’re capturing real life. Imagine using an AI image of made-up sailors instead of sailors that are actually doing the job.”
Another said: “AI can’t replicate what you can do. We can’t go out on the ground. We can’t search out human interest stories. AI can’t find them things. There’s got to be a face out there.”
A third made the case in terms of reach: “Photography is such a powerful medium. We don’t need words for our pictures. Our pictures can communicate to somebody who doesn’t speak English, doesn’t speak French, doesn’t speak Urdu.”
The film also features James Clark, team leader of the video production unit, a specialist team within the photographic branch producing scripted films to the First Sea Lord’s strategic direction. Its output includes the Silent Night Christmas video following Diamond’s Red Sea deployment and a nine-minute film on Royal Marines raiding.
He said: “The projects that we’ve done have gone down so well because they’re made by people who are serving, so we’ve got a good idea of what people want to see, and I think that gives a real authenticity to every film.”
Work from the unit has appeared on Piccadilly Circus, in cinemas and on billboards nationwide.
The film was made by the photographers themselves and released to mark World Photography Day. It can be watched below.

articles.title: ‘Don’t Even Think About It’: Ex-Danish FM Warns Russia Amid NATO Drills
articles.body:
Nordic countries are “ready to respond” should Russia provoke NATO, former Danish Foreign Minister Jeppe Kofod told TVP World, as long-planned NATO military exercises got underway near Russia’s Kaliningrad exclave.
“We have to be resilient. We have to rehearse our military forces,” Kofod said on TVP World’s World News Tonight program.

The exercises in Poland, he said, show Moscow that “if they provoke us, we are ready to respond.”
“So, they shouldn’t even think about that idea,” he added, saying the participation of US forces also demonstrated that Washington “is still very present in Europe, and that is good for our security.”
The exercises opened with a flyby of US jets around Kaliningrad, a strategically sensitive area wedged between Poland and Lithuania.
But while Kofod praised “exponential” military build-up in the Nordic countries in recent years, he warned they had to keep the initiative.
More work to do
“I think we have to build up much faster than we have done before,” he said, calling for NATO countries to reach 5% of GDP in defense spending “the sooner the better.”
Kofod also highlighted the urgent need for stronger air defenses, pointing to Russia’s deadly attack on Kyiv on Thursday, which killed at least 16 people.
Russia Unleashes 135 Drones on Ukraine, Killing 2 in Kharkiv Region and Injuring 6 in Sumy
He said Nordic leaders, who gathered on Thursday in the Danish capital of Copenhagen, were discussing “common air defense as one of the solutions,” arguing that closer cooperation could pool national capabilities.
“Each country has military assets,” he said. “Poland has a lot of military assets, and if you bring them together, then Russia will have no chance.”
The former minister also called for greater protection of critical infrastructure, including electricity grids, pipelines and oil facilities, as Russia continues what he described as hybrid warfare.
He said Europe must also increase its own ability to defend itself while continuing to support Ukraine, particularly with air defense systems, warning that Russia could intensify attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure ahead of winter.

Poland has summoned Israel’s ambassador to express its “great disappointment” that the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) have discontinued an investigation into the strikes on an aid convoy in Gaza in 2024 that killed seven humanitarian workers, including a Pole, Damian Soból.
“Partnership requires mutual respect,” declared foreign minister Radosław Sikorski. “The humanitarian catastrophe in Gaza, as well as the failure of accountability for [the] IDF’s excessive use of force[,] are undermining public support in even pro-Israel nations.”
Partnership requires mutual respect. The humanitarian catastrophe in Gaza, as well as the failure of accountability for IDF’s excessive use of force are undermining public support in even pro-Israel nations. https://t.co/9H0nhiDE4H
— Radosław Sikorski 🇵🇱🇪🇺 (@sikorskiradek) August 20, 2026
The incident in question took place in April 2024, when Israeli drones struck a convoy delivering humanitarian aid from World Central Kitchen (WCK), a major international food relief NGO. The attack killed seven aid workers, including Soból.
The incident caused outrage in Poland, whose government demanded that Israel fully explain the circumstances. The IDF expressed “sincere sorrow” over the deaths and pledged to carry out a “thorough and transparent” investigation.
On Wednesday this week, the IDF announced that it had closed the case after determining “no reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct that would justify the opening of a criminal investigation or the taking of additional measures against any of those involved in the incident”.
The IDF said that its troops had identified a gunman on one of the trucks in the convoy. It also claimed that WCK had hired an armed security force to protect the convoy without coordinating that with IDF authorities and that the convoy deviated from the route previously agreed with the IDF.
However, the IDF also acknowledged that it had mistakenly identified several individuals as being armed. It added that attempts to contact WCK representatives over a half-hour period while the convoy was on the move were unsuccessful.
The IDF noted that, after the incident, two military officers were removed from their positions while three others were reprimanded. But it found that there was no basis for any further action.

On Thursday, Poland’s foreign ministry issued a statement saying that it was “greatly disappointed to receive the information provided about the discontinuation of the proceedings by the Israeli military authorities”.
It announced that it had summoned the Israeli ambassador in order to “communicate a critical assessment of the actions taken to date to clarify the causes and course of the tragedy”.
It also noted that Polish prosecutors are still conducting their own investigation and that the foreign ministry had informed the Israeli ambassador that they “expect the Israeli side will provide the relevant Polish authorities with all necessary explanations and materials requested”.
“The circumstances of the tragedy should be fully investigated and [we] do not accept that the perpetrators are avoiding legal and moral responsibility,” concluded the ministry, adding that “the families deserve adequate compensation”.
We strongly condemn the Israeli military prosecutor’s account of the deaths of our seven colleagues on April 1, 2024. And we fundamentally disagree with their decision about criminal investigations into the IDF airstrikes that killed our team.
Read our full statement here:…
— World Central Kitchen (@WCKitchen) August 19, 2026
The IDF’s findings were also condemned by WCK itself, which called them “inconsistent with the full truth and deeply offensive”. It added that, “at the time of the lethal attacks, the IDF knew that our team in Gaza was unarmed and posing a threat to nobody”.
The NGO repeated its demand for an independent investigation into the incident, “because the IDF cannot credibly investigate its own conduct”.
On Friday, the UK, Canada and Australia, whose citizens were also killed in the strike, issued a joint statement calling the IDF’s decision to drop the investigation “shameful” and another example of the lack of accountability for incidents in Gaza.

articles.title: BNN IN FOCUS | “Arrogant officials don’t understand” – CSDD data leak also poses a threat to democracy
articles.body:
The cyberattack on Latvia’s Road Traffic Safety Directorate (CSDD) and the leak of data belonging to 1.2 million residents show that Latvia is largely prepared for various crises only “on paper”. In fact, the situation is even worse – a security vulnerability in CSDD’s IT system could have been fixed several years ago, but instead CSDD took the person who discovered it to court. As a result, Latvia is where it is today, with its preparedness for crises and military threats rated at just four out of ten. BNN asked political scientist and co-owner of Mediju tilts Filips Rajevskis what needs to be done to prevent such situations in the future.
“Crisis preparedness begins with the way we approach very basic things, from shelters to procedures for what to do if a drone is approaching,” Rajevskis says. “Let’s be realistic – a drone is not the fastest thing that can come flying at us. Missiles can also arrive, including ballistic missiles, which travel much faster and can cause considerably greater damage. Crisis preparedness also depends heavily on how we approach other issues. And in the CSDD case, we can see quite clearly the attitude towards our data, which is vitally important. If an enemy uses this data, it can obtain an enormous amount of information about the people who live here, their daily routines and their lives.”
Rajevskis stresses that it is precisely this attitude towards matters of critical importance to national security that also affects assessments of Latvia’s preparedness for crises and military threats.
“We saw that, in the initial stage of the CSDD crisis, the management board, which later resigned, approached the situation with an attitude along the lines of: what’s the big deal? From publicly available information, we can see that they had previously dismissed warnings that the data was not sufficiently protected and that there were risks. If I am not mistaken, this may be the first time in Latvia’s history that the President has turned to the Prosecutor’s Office over the actions of the CSDD management board. I do not recall presidents filing such complaints with prosecutors in other cases. It shows the outrage of both the President and the Prime Minister following the closed Cabinet meeting, when it was said that they were being lied to their faces. This shows that we do not even need an external enemy – internal actors who negligently handle data that is, in reality, an extremely important resource and must be protected are enough.
This can affect Latvia’s defence capabilities and security.”
Responding to BNN’s observation that it is currently difficult to predict the consequences of the leak involving data on 1.2 million individuals and 200,000 legal entities, Rajevskis says: “If we exclude babies and children who have not yet reached the age at which they receive their first identity documents, then practically everyone else was in there. A very large number of people have a driving licence or some other connection with CSDD.”
Asked to what extent the case highlights questions about the usefulness of various supervisory and management boards, the political scientist says that before discussing their usefulness, it is important to focus on these people’s attitude towards their work and the responsibilities entrusted to them.
“In this case, the CSDD management board was responsible for the data placed in its care. That is directly their responsibility.”
Asked to comment on the case of inventor Raimonds Skuruls, who warned CSDD several years ago about a security vulnerability and, instead of being thanked, was taken to court on extortion charges, Rajevskis says the issue once again comes down to attitude.
“Perhaps it is also connected to the high salaries –
people become so detached from society and so arrogant that they ignore warning signs.
The question now is who will cover the losses. They are enormous. This is not simply a case of data going missing somewhere. The data leak will also result in financial losses. Who will pay for them – the taxpayers? And this brings us back to the responsibility of the management board. The high salaries paid to board members are justified on the grounds that board members are accountable for their actions. This is one of those moments when accountability should actually work, considering the large salaries these people have received for years.”
Asked whether such accountability will actually work, or whether instead there will be cries that “democracy is under threat” because officials are being asked to cover the losses, Rajevskis responds:
“Democracy really is under threat. A great many people use e-CSDD, and the data includes people’s addresses as well as their official electronic addresses. This information can be used to manipulate society and, consequently, democracy itself.”
Finally, asked whether the case will serve as a sufficiently powerful lesson for other state institutions to start paying greater attention to data security, Rajevskis says:
“Seeing the enormous arrogance displayed by the CSDD management board in the early stages, I am going to be pessimistic.”

articles.title: Ukraine’s new commander spoke with chair of NATO’s Military Committee. Result: body will visit Ukraine in October, for first time in eight years
articles.body:
NATO's top military body is coming to Ukraine for the first time in nearly a decade. NATO's Military Committee will visit Ukraine in October, the last such visit having been eight years ago, Commander-in-Chief Mykhailo Drapatyi said after his first conversation with Admiral Giuseppe Cavo Dragone, the committee's chair, the General Staff reported.
Coming early in Drapatyi's tenure as commander-in-chief, the plans on the first NATO Military Committee trip to Ukraine reflect an alliance drawing closer to a country that both receives its support and feeds back combat experience no other NATO member has.
Drapatyi briefed NATO on the front and Ukraine's priorities
Drapatyi laid out the war for the alliance's top soldier. He informed Cavo Dragone about the situation at the front and Ukraine's priorities: long-range strikes, flexible infantry tactics, and the robotization of the front line, according to the General Staff.
Air defense was a focus. Drapatyi stressed that protecting the skies is his priority amid the same interceptor-shortage problem that has left Ukrainian cities exposed to Russian missiles. He thanked the admiral for his consistent support, noting Cavo Dragone had visited Ukraine three times and seen the situation firsthand.
Ukraine frames itself as a contributor
Drapatyi cast the relationship as two-way.
"In October, we expect the NATO Military Committee in Ukraine. The last such visit was eight years ago. Ukraine not only receives support. We transfer combat experience that no one has today, and it works for the security of the whole Alliance," he said.
The admiral confirmed continued support
Cavo Dragone affirmed NATO's backing. He confirmed NATO's continued military support as Ukraine defends its sovereignty and territorial integrity, and said allies in Europe and North America are ramping up defense production, speeding deliveries, and supporting the transfer of needed equipment to Ukraine, he wrote on X.
"I have seen Ukrainian courage with my own eyes: soldiers holding the line with extraordinary bravery for their homes, their families, and their freedom," Dragone said.
He tied Ukraine's security to the alliance's own.
"Ukraine's security is our security, and we will continue to stand alongside Ukraine to help achieve a just and lasting peace," he added.

articles.title: Ukrainian drones attack Russia’s Perm
articles.body:
Ukrainian drones attack Russia’s Perm
Perm declared a drone threat alert on the morning of August 21, as sirens sounded and residents reported explosions. The city’s airport suspended all flights.
Perm Krai authorities had provided no information about the aftermath of the attack by the time of publication. Astra, an independent Telegram channel, reported smoke rising over the Lukoil-Permnefteorgsintez oil refinery — one of Russia’s largest, and a repeated target of Ukrainian drone strikes.
Russia’s Defense Ministry announced that its air defenses had shot down 325 drones over Russian regions overnight. Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said seven of them had been flying toward the capital.
Perm sits about 1,400 kilometers (870 miles) from the Ukrainian border. Ukrainian drones have struck the city’s oil refinery several times since the spring of 2026 and hit a Wildberries warehouse there in June.

articles.title: Türkiye’s ROKETSAN aims to end foreign dependence with homegrown solutions
articles.body:
Ali Atar
21 August 2026•Update: 21 August 2026
Turkish defense firm ROKETSAN aims to develop homegrown guided munitions to empower domestic platforms, while the indigenous Atmaca anti-ship missile’s integration into frigates and other domestic corvettes has eliminated foreign reliance in this area. 
ROKETSAN CEO Murat Ikinci addressed recent developments while speaking on the sidelines of the ongoing naval defense expo TEKNOFEST Blue Homeland.
Türkiye’s four-day naval defense event kicked off on Thursday to showcase the country’s diverse naval capabilities, underwater technology and defense industry while hosting competitions for budding engineers.
Anadolu is the global communications partner of the event, where a wide range of products and technologies are on display, ranging from various classes of Turkish Navy platforms to unmanned systems and from aircraft to air defense and missile systems.
Ikinci said ROKETSAN’s Akya heavy-class torpedo provided the Turkish submarine fleet with striking power without relying on foreign providers.
He noted that the firm also integrated the Akata system into submarines to enable them to launch Atmaca cruise missiles.
Ikinci said the integration of the Siper and Hisar missiles into the national vertical launch system MIDLAS has already been completed.
“Meanwhile, testing and trials of the close-in air missile system Levent are underway, for which we expect a massive export success, especially in the Gulf region amid the Iran-Israel war,” he said.
“All these efforts for our navy not only reduce and eliminate Türkiye’s foreign dependence but also create an alternative resource in the field for allied countries,” he added.
Ikinci said integrating guided missiles into armored unmanned surface vehicles is key to enhancing their capabilities, and ROKETSAN’s Cirit, Sungur, Cakir and L-UMTAS missiles act as a force multiplier for the Turkish Navy.

articles.title: Russia conducts missile test near Kuril Islands after Japanese protest
articles.body:
Russia conducts missile test near Kuril Islands after Japanese protest
The Russian Navy has carried out a successful missile test near the country’s Kuril Islands, the Pacific Fleet has said.
The test comes a week after Japan vigorously protested Russian President Vladimir Putin’s first-ever visit to the archipelago, which is partially claimed by Tokyo.
The missile test, which took place near the southern Kurils, involved the Varyag guided missile cruiser, the Omsk nuclear-powered submarine, and a ground-based Bastion surface-to-ship missile system, the Russian Pacific Fleet said in a statement on Thursday.
They fired several types of munitions at a target simulating enemy vessels at a distance of around 300 km (186 miles), with targeting data provided by naval aviation, the fleet said.
Objective control data confirmed the destruction of all targets, it stressed.
Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi reacted to the drills by telling reporters that Tokyo “cannot tolerate moves [by Russia] to strengthen military power on the four Northern Islands because they go against our country’s stance [on the territories].”
Kyodo news earlier reported that Japan had lodged a protest with Russia after Moscow notified it of the upcoming missile test last week.
On Tuesday, the Russian Foreign Ministry summoned Tokyo’s ambassador to Moscow to express a strong protest over “anti-Russian statements” by the Japanese leadership.
After Putin traveled to Iturup, the largest of the Kuril Islands, on August 13, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi called the trip “absolutely unacceptable” and said it “hurts the feelings of the Japanese people.” Motegi also issued a statement, claiming that the four southernmost islands of the archipelago “are an inherent part of Japan’s territory both historically and under international law.”
The Russian Foreign Ministry said it informed the Japanese envoy that “Russia’s sovereignty and jurisdiction over the southern Kuril Islands are inviolable. These territories were transferred to our country following World War II, as enshrined in the relevant agreements of the Allied Powers and the UN Charter.”
“Any attempts by the Japanese side to directly or indirectly call this obvious reality into question are categorically unacceptable and illegitimate,” it added.
Moscow “reserves the right to take appropriate countermeasures” in response to Japan’s adherence to Western sanctions against Russia and its support for Ukraine, the ministry warned.
The Kuril Islands, stretching from Kamchatka to Japan’s Hokkaido, came under Soviet control following Tokyo’s defeat in World War II and were subsequently incorporated into the USSR. The Japanese authorities, however, continue to claim the islands of Iturup, Kunashir, Shikotan, and the Habomai – which they call the “Northern Territories.” The dispute has been the main obstacle to Moscow and Tokyo signing a formal peace treaty in the eight decades since the conflict.
